articles.title_orig: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.title_zh: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.content_orig:
Jorge Dubcovsky, a wheat geneticist at the University of California, Davis, has been named the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate in the category for countries with developed economies.
The award recognizes his contributions to wheat improvement and global food security. It is presented by the Global Confederation of Higher Education Associations for the Agricultural and Life Sciences, known as GCHERA.
Dubcovsky is a distinguished professor in the UC Davis Department of Plant Sciences and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute researcher, according to a press release.
For more than three decades, Dubcovsky’s research has advanced understanding of wheat biology and helped breeding programs apply genomic tools to crop improvement.
His work has identified and characterized genes controlling yield, disease resistance, flowering time, nutrient use efficiency and adaptation to different growing environments. Those discoveries have contributed to improved wheat varieties grown on millions of hectares worldwide.
“The World Agriculture Prize recognizes individuals whose achievements have had a profound and lasting impact on global agriculture and human well-being,” said Doug Steele, chair of the World Agriculture Prize International Committee. “Dubcovsky’s scientific leadership and extraordinary contributions to wheat genetics have strengthened the resilience of one of the world’s most important food crops and have delivered tangible benefits to farmers, food systems and society. His work exemplifies the innovation, excellence, and global impact that the prize seeks to honor.”
Dubcovsky has worked with researchers, breeding institutions, governments and international agricultural organizations to move wheat discoveries into practical use. He has also mentored plant scientists and breeders who continue to contribute to crop research and development.
The World Agriculture Prize recognizes contributions to agriculture and food security through research, innovation, leadership and service. GCHERA also recognizes scientists from countries not classified as having developed economies.
Dubcovsky will be formally honored Oct. 28 at the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Award Ceremony at Nanjing Agricultural University in China.

articles.title_orig: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Starbucks enters Xinjiang in calculated geopolitical risk
articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Starbucks enters Xinjiang in calculated geopolitical risk
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Anniek, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Starbucks struck one of Asia's most closely watched deals last year, selling a majority stake in its China business to a local private-equity firm. Now it is getting headaches at home over choices made by a partner that increasingly leans toward Beijing's priorities.
Starbucks Corp has taken its green apron to Xinjiang, a region where Western governments accuse Beijing of widespread human-rights abuses and where the U.S. restricts imports over forced-labor concerns.
The opening of two stores in Urumqi shows how the Chinese private-equity firm that now controls Starbucks' business in its second-largest market is willing to weather Washington's anger.
Starbucks completed the sale of a 60% controlling stake in its China operations to Boyu Capital in April. The venture aims to grow from roughly 8,000 stores to as many as 20,000, and Xinjiang appears to be a bold, if controversial, first stop.
The U.S. House Select Committee on China called the decision "shocking and morally bankrupt" for "a company that prides itself on social responsibility" and demanded the stores close. Its chairman, Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), was blunt in that statement headlined "Starbucks Serves Up Venti-Sized Genocide."
China's Foreign Ministry rejected the criticism, calling U.S. claims of genocide "a blatant lie" and saying Xinjiang has emerged as a region of "social stability, economic prosperity, ethnic unity and religious harmony." Beijing has long defended its security crackdown as necessary to counter terrorism and religious extremism, and denies allegations of "crimes against humanity" and ongoing repression.
Boyu — run by people who know China's politics well — wouldn't have missed the risk, said Ivy Yang, founder of Wavelet Strategy. "Boyu understands the sensitivity of Xinjiang as well as anyone," she said. In her view, the decision shows the firm weighed Washington's reaction and concluded that the domestic commercial opportunity mattered more.
The Hong Kong-based private-equity firm, co-founded by Alvin Jiang, a grandson of the late President Jiang Zemin, has long been seen as having close ties to China's political elite.
Starbucks has been losing ground on price and speed to local rivals, Yang said, and a new owner who's under pressure to deliver growth is likely to go where the stores aren't yet.
Molly Liu, chief executive of Starbucks China, in a recent statement , pledged to keep investing in the region.
Some, however, believe Starbucks' store openings cannot be read as a purely commercial decision.
"Chinese authorities have a strong interest in attracting prominent global brands to Xinjiang to demonstrate the region's stability," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.
Beijing has spent years courting investment in Xinjiang. Supporting the region economically became a state goal after the controversy over Xinjiang cotton, said Yaling Jiang, founder of consumer consulting firm ApertureChina, and state television and social-media content have since turned it into a consumer aspiration.
But Xinjiang remains among China's poorer regions. Its full-year rural per capita disposable income only just topped 20,000 yuan ($2,983) for the first time last year, compared with 24,456 yuan for rural residents nationwide. The non-metropolitan median household income in the U.S. was $60,459 in 2023.
More than a dozen American brands have already ventured into Xinjiang, including Pizza Hut, KFC, McDonald's, Tesla and Burger King. But few have drawn comparable criticism from U.S. lawmakers.
And that expansion has gathered pace since 2023, according to GeoHey Brand Insights, a geospatial-data research firm, despite the landmark Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act signed into law in December 2021.
"Worsening geopolitics is inevitable, and must be priced into any exit negotiation," said Meng Shen, director of Chanson & Co., a Beijing-based boutique investment bank, of multinationals' interest in joint ventures with Chinese partners.
With U.S.-China ties steadying this year, Starbucks' Xinjiang stores are now a test of the climate for American business in China, Wang said — if Starbucks ultimately halts the project under U.S. pressure, it would send a negative signal to American businesses in China that commercial commitments can be overridden by political pressure from Washington.
That could make U.S. brands even more wary of Chinese partners and future deals harder to negotiate, she said.
'Unwelcome and unsafe': Why Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate
Japanese companies are leaving China in record numbers , as a slowing Chinese economy and a diplomatic freeze force businesses to reassess their presence in the world's second-largest economy.
China wants in on U.S. AI data center boom. Here's why
Chinese manufacturers are eyeing the U.S. data center buildout as an opportunity, even as the two countries compete for AI dominance. "We can see very big potential in the U.S. market," said S.K. Lee, a global vice president at Singapore-registered Brightray, an AI infrastructure company. "The China market is equally important, but we can see that there's a stronger demand in the U.S."
Big Pharma's China deal spree grows with latest tie-up worth up to $7.8 billion
Novartis signed a deal worth up to $7.8 billion with China-based Abogen Biosciences for an mRNA therapy for autoimmune disease, the latest in a run of tie-ups between Big Pharma and Chinese biotechs.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court grapples with case on holding Big Oil liable for climate change
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Trump says taxpayer money will no longer be used for campaign-style TV ads promoting him, a major reversal after bipartisan criticism
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court kicked off a new term Monday, with the justices wrestling with an attempt by oil companies to throw out lawsuits alleging they should pay damages for the impacts of climate change .
Although the case concerns a specific lawsuit the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, brought against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, the ultimate decision could have broad ramifications for more than two dozen similar lawsuits brought by cities and counties around the country.
The justices — lacking a ninth member because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself — asked tough questions of both sides as they tackled broad legal questions raised in the case. Alito’s absence raises the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling that would leave the legal issues unresolved while allowing the Boulder case to move forward.
Boulder officials say they face increasing costs because of the impacts of climate change, including efforts to minimize risks from wildfires. Just this summer, Colorado has experienced extreme heat, drought and multiple fires .
The lawsuit, bringing claims under state law, says Exxon and Suncor misled consumers about the impact that greenhouse gases produced by their products would have on the climate.
The companies deny the allegations and warn that if the Boulder lawsuit and others like it are able to move forward to trial, they and other energy companies could face crippling damages in the billions of dollars. They also argue climate change is such an inherently national and international issue that it cannot be the subject of litigation in state courts.
There was some sympathy from the bench toward the oil companies and the potential for substantial damages.
Chief Justice John Roberts, one of the court’s conservatives, wondered how many more cities and counties would launch similar lawsuits if the court allows the Boulder case to continue.
“Just to make sure I have a correct understanding. Presumably, if you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” he told Boulder’s lawyer, Kevin Russell.
Although Boulder’s claims are based on consumer deception, Roberts also seemed skeptical that the lawsuit was anything other than what he called “an effort to reduce emissions.”
On the other hand, Roberts, in an exchange with the oil companies’ lawyer, Kannon Shanmugam, said litigation brought in state court against out-of-state companies over an alleged harmful product is commonplace.
Other justices also seemed conflicted. Liberal Justice Elena Kagan at one point compared climate litigation with the wave of lawsuits against tobacco companies and drug manufacturers that sold opioids, which were allowed to proceed.
The oil companies have pushed back on such comparisons, saying that in the tobacco and opioid litigation there was a much more direct connection between the product and alleged harm to consumers.
But Kagan also wondered whether, as the oil companies argue, the Clean Air Act, which Congress passed to regulate air emissions nationwide, could foreclose the Boulder claims. A ruling saying state lawsuits are pre-empted by the federal law could be “the more natural and simpler route” of deciding the case if the court sides with the companies, she said.
A decision on those lines would be the narrower of two paths to victory for the oil companies, with Shanmugam pushing for a broader ruling that state lawsuits are prohibited under the Constitution.
Liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor pointed out that even if the Clean Air Act bars states from seeking to cap emissions, the lawsuit does not seek to do that. “The Clean Air Act does not regulate marketing or advertising of fuel, correct?” she said.
The most vocal justice in backing the oil companies was conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who cited several court precedents that he said were “crystal clear” that air and water pollution are matters of federal law that the states cannot regulate.
“We don’t have to reinvent the wheel, because we’ve said this multiple times,” he added.
Overall, there appeared to be a lack of consensus on the bench about how to resolve the case, with one possibility that the court simply dismisses it, which would allow litigation to continue.
Lurking in the background are recent efforts by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency to eliminate greenhouse gas regulations under the Clean Air Act, an issue being litigated that could reach the justices in a later case.
“I think it is difficult to decide whether the Clean Air Act pre-empts these claims when we don’t know whether the Clean Air Act applies to greenhouse gas emissions when the EPA is saying it lacks the statutory authority to do that,” Russell told the justices.
The Boulder case was the first to be argued in the courtroom as the justices began a new nine-month term after a summer break. Other major cases already on the docket involve a challenge to bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles and two about the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies .
Alito announced last week he was stepping aside from hearing the Boulder lawsuit but did not say why. Liberal groups have said for months that he should recuse himself because he owns stocks in other oil companies that could benefit from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor. Alito’s decision was a surprise, as the court had told NBC News in May there was no need for him to step aside.
The litigation is playing out amid a broader battle between oil companies and their allies on one side and groups advocating for action on climate change on the other.
State courts have become a focus, in part, because of a lack of action at the federal level, with the Trump administration rolling back Obama- and Biden-era policies seeking to reduce carbon emissions and speed up the transition to cleaner energy. The administration, which filed a brief backing Exxon and Suncor, has also sought to block renewable energy projects, with President Donald Trump calling climate change a “hoax.”
In a ruling in 2011 , the Supreme Court shut the door to making certain claims against energy companies over climate change in federal court, saying they were displaced by the Clean Air Act.
The proxy war over the issue has also focused attention on a chapter about climate science in a reference manual for federal judges. It was abruptly withdrawn this year after conservatives alleged the authors had a conflict of interest. Some also called for Kagan to recuse herself in Monday’s case because she wrote a foreword to the manual. She later said she did not even read the climate chapter.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
articles.title_zh: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
All 12 American bombers deployed in Britain rapidly returned to the U.S. on Oct. 4 following security concerns about a potential Iranian threat to their base in the U.K.
The dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which were stationed at RAF Fairford amid ongoing hostilities with Iran, departed over the course of a day, local aircraft spotters said. The U.S. military later confirmed the unexpected departure of the aircraft.
“All U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” the Pentagon and U.S. European Command said in statements to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The U.S. military emphasized that bombers could still strike targets across the globe from the continental United States—something B-1B, B-2 Spirit , and B-52 Stratofortress bombers all did during the height of operations against Iran this spring.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities—including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States—anywhere, anytime,” the statement read.
Still, stationing bombers at RAF Fairford sharply reduced the flight time U.S. bombers needed to strike targets in Iran. The open-source group Military Air Tracking Alliance recorded 29 separate bombers that deployed to RAF Fairford, located in southwest England, at different points during the conflict.
The departure of the last 12 bombers comes a week after arrests were made following a suspected plot against the base. Six people have been arrested in connection with the episode. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran was behind the threat .
Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer allowed the U.S. to use the base to attack Iran for what the U.K. government called defensive strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July it considered RAF Fairford a legitimate target because of the U.S. bombers deployed there.
At the height of the deployment, which began in early March during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. had around two dozen bombers deployed to RAF Fairford at a single time—some 18 B-1B and half a dozen B-52H bombers. Since the U.S. reached a shaky ceasefire with Iran in April, the bombers have mostly conducted training missions, and the B-52s left months ago. One B-1B that arrived just last week to replace another bomber was part of the exodus on Oct. 4.
RAF Fairford does not have permanent assigned U.S. Air Force aircraft, but the base has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
The Air Force permanently stations aircraft in the U.K. at RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath also serves as a stopover for fighters heading to and from the Middle East from the U.S. Nearby, RAF Mildenhall hosts KC-135 tankers that belong to the 100th Air Refueling Wing stationed at the base.
The U.S. has also been rotating its fighters based in the Middle East, sending fresh F-16 Fighting Falcon and F-35 units to the region, primarily from the Air National Guard.

articles.title_orig: US seeks to revoke citizenship of two China-born men convicted in Beijing-linked cases
articles.title_zh: US seeks to revoke citizenship of two China-born men convicted in Beijing-linked cases
articles.content_orig:
Former US Navy sailor Jinchao Wei and Florida resident Ping Li are among 40 people named in DOJ announcement
Jinchao Wei and Ping Li are among 40 people facing denaturalisation actions in what the department described as the largest batch of such filings under the Trump administration. The civil proceedings remain pending, with no determination of liability, the DOJ said.
The case against Wei was filed on September 30 in the Southern District of California, while the case against Li was filed on October 1 in the Middle District of Florida.
Wei was convicted of espionage and export offences in August 2025 and sentenced in January to 200 months in prison, or 16 years and eight months. But the same jury acquitted him of naturalisation fraud, according to the DOJ’s announcement of his sentence.

articles.title_orig: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.title_zh: 2 People, Including Winter Haven High School Student, Killed in Florida Bus Crash
articles.content_orig:
Two people were killed after a major school bus crash in Winter Haven on Monday morning, according to the Polk County Sheriff's Office.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said the incident happened around 6:15 a.m.
He said the school bus was traveling eastbound on Lucerne Park Road when a westbound white Chevy Malibu crashed into it.
Judd said the impact caused the bus to lose control and tear off a tire. The bus then collided head-on with a Jeep and ultimately overturned.
As a result, two people were killed, including a 10th-grade student.
In addition to the school bus, three other vehicles were involved in the crash.
The school bus was carrying 39 people, including 37 high school students, who were on their way to Winter Haven High School.
The other two people on the bus were identified as the school bus driver and the driver's 9-year-old daughter.
The Winter Haven Police Department said Lucerne Park Road was shut down in both directions at US-27. It has since reopened.
The Winter Haven Hospital confirmed it received 22 patients, including 19 pediatric patients and 3 adults.
The hospital said it has treated and released all patients except one pediatric patient who was transferred to another hospital.
Polk County Public Schools confirmed the school bus involved in the crash did have seatbelts for students, adding that all of the school district's buses are equipped with lap belts.
"A PCPS school bus was involved in a serious accident this morning in Winter Haven, which claimed the life of a Winter Haven High student and another motorist.
This is devastating news for WHHS and our community. We are praying for the victims and their families. Thank you to the many dedicated first responders who provided essential support this morning."
>> See full news conference below:
The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation into the crash in coordination with the sheriff's office.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump told Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson on Monday that he thinks Iran was behind the attempted attack aboard a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight on Sept. 30.
“And on flydubai. Do you think Iran was responsible for that terrorist attack?” Tomlinson asked.
President Trump said, “I do, I personally do.”
The Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight had landed safely in Saudi Arabia after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who attacked the captain and tried to crash the plane.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said Monday that one of its staff members who had been detained by the Houthis in Yemen was released and reunited with his family.
“We stand in solidarity with the 72 U.N. personnel and five former U.N. personnel, including WFP colleagues, who remain detained in Yemen, and will continue to pursue every possible avenue to secure their immediate and safe release,” the program said in a statement.
WFP joined the U.N. secretary-general in calling for the release of all detained U.N. personnel and other humanitarian workers in Yemen, it added.
U.S. Central Command ( CENTCOM ) said Monday that its forces have redirected 130 ships since the start of its blockade of Iranian ports.
It also confirmed that it had destroyed 13 ships that were violating the blockade or were part of IRGC's multibillion-dollar shadow network.
“The U.S. military remains intensely focused on this mission,” CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a post on X .
“We will swiftly act against any vessels trying to run the blockade. Our forces are highly trained, professional, and lethal,” he added.
Norway’s Christian Democratic Party has proposed to establish its own terror blacklist, which would include Hamas, Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, The Jerusalem Post .
Norway does not have its own terrorist organization list, instead relying on the UN sanctions framework.
Parliament will vote on whether to instruct the government to develop a system for creating the list, the outlet said. If approved, the government would determine its legal and administrative framework.
“We have been working on this for some time,” Christian Democratic Party lawmaker Joel Ystebø told The Jerusalem Post.
“The reason why we are putting forward this proposal is that many of our allies have their own lists, and we think that would be very good for Norway, too, because it is important to take a stand when it comes to terrorism and antisemitism.."
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces shared a video Monday showing their forces targeting Houthi militia amid reports that the port of Mocha had been recaptured.
“Targeting by our armed forces of elements of the Houthi terrorist militia and its military equipment within Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen,’” the spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces said on X .
This came as the Defense Ministry said its armed forces had recaptured Mocha, which the Houthis seized last month.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki also said Monday that 100 fighter jets were involved in Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” with forces destroying 324 high-value Houthi targets.
Washington moved 12 American bombers from RAF Fairford in the U.K. on Sunday amid concerns about a potentially complex drone attack ordered by the IRGC, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday.
Citing officials, the outlet reported the planned attack was part of a plot to target the aircraft and kill personnel at the base, including American pilots.
“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well,” Vice President JD Vance said Monday. “We are being extremely cautious.”
When pressed by reporters on the tarmac before departing for Grand Island, Nebraska, about whether Iran had brought combat drones into the United Kingdom, President Donald Trump replied, “I can't tell you that,” before stating, “But if they did, they'll suffer greatly.”
The U.K. arrested and released on bail six men over the suspected terror plot as the investigation continues.
The United States, Paraguay, and eight other Western nations issued a joint statement Monday condemning Iranian terrorist activity across the region.
The declaration , which followed a co-hosted Countering Transnational Terrorism Forum between the U.S. and Paraguay, called on Tehran and its proxies to immediately halt all hostile operations.
The nations highlighted ongoing threats including lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, foreign political interference, and efforts to strengthen regional terrorist networks.
The coalition includes Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, and the U.S.
“This is part of the Trump Administration’s ongoing efforts to reinforce our joint resolve to safeguard our hemisphere’s safety and security,” the State Department said.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued a warning Monday to foreign financial institutions, stating that any continued business with Iran or its financial sector could trigger immediate sanctions without prior notice.
“Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should take immediate action to terminate such activity and relationships,” the Treasury Department said.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday that its forces carried out a military operation in Hodeida province as well as launching a major offensive against the Houthis in the region, Reuters reported.
According to Col. Turki Al-Maliki, the official spokesman for coalition forces, the operation was “to protect maritime navigation security in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.”
“We destroyed weapons depots, boat explosive storage facilities, and naval mines,” Al-Maliki said on X .
“We have thwarted a plot for imminent attacks targeting the waterways south of the Red Sea,” he said, adding that the operation included the “destruction of legitimate military targets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia.”
"The naval forces of the Coalition carried out a military operation in Al Hudaydah Governorate," Al-Maliki added.
Explosions were heard across the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Monday, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported on X.
Reuters also reported that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they carried out three military operations targeting several locations in Saudi Arabia , including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha International Airport and the Khamis Mushait military base.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia, the outlet reported.
U.S. sanctions successfully froze Iranian oil exports completely last month as the country's currency plunged to record lows, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday.
“Operation Economic Outcast is delivering results: the rial has plunged to record lows, Iran loaded zero crude oil onto tankers last month, and even Iran’s top security official has admitted the country is facing one of the most difficult periods in its history,” Bessent said on X .
“The Iranian regime allows its own people to suffer while it pours resources into terrorism,” he added before vowing that Operation Economic Outcast would not stop until the Iranian regime understands that Washington “will never allow the regime to fund terrorism and develop a nuclear weapon.”
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) is pushing back against claims that it purposely targets journalists in Gaza , stating that individuals "presented as innocent journalists" were actually in Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) and other terrorist organizations.
"They presented themselves as legitimate media professionals while serving terrorist organizations that regularly use propaganda and psychological warfare," the IDF stated on its website.

articles.title_orig: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
articles.title_zh: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
articles.content_orig:
President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month ahead of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday, Trump shrugged off questions about his approval ratings.
“I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who’d asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media.
But according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll release Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance.
Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despite even conservative states starting to show the loss of support. Some Republicans have also started to distance themselves from the president over issues like immigration as they attempt to hold onto local support.
With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.

articles.title_orig: Entergy Texas Names David Borde President and CEO
articles.title_zh: Entergy Texas Names David Borde President and CEO
articles.content_orig:
Electric utility company Entergy Texas has appointed a new president and CEO to head the company’s broader customer-centric strategies following the departure of former CEO Eliecer Viamontes.
On Monday, Entergy Texas announced that David Borde will now lead the company. The move comes as Viamontes departed for other opportunities, according to a company release.
Headshot of new president and CEO David Borde. | Credit: Entergy Texas
Prior to accepting the role as president and CEO, Borde, who joined Entergy in 2009, served as the company’s vice president of utility strategy and regulatory initiatives. In that role, he supported Entergy’s objectives by leading regulatory and tariff filing efforts while  providing ongoing strategic and regulatory counsel.
During his tenure, Borde held several other key leadership roles, including serving as director of corporate development based in Texas, vice president of investor relations and within the utility finance business partner organization.
The company noted that this regulatory focus has allowed the organization to keep pace with evolving customer needs.
“David has extensive experience in utility strategy, regulatory affairs and utility finance, along with his deep understanding of our business and customers,” said Drew Marsh, chair and CEO of Entergy. “He is a thoughtful and proven leader, and he will build on the strong foundation in Texas while advancing our commitment to providing safe, reliable and affordable energy to the communities we serve.”
Before joining Entergy, Borde worked in the investment banking division of Citigroup USA and as a lawyer at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. He earned a Juris Doctor degree from Duke University’s School of Law in 2001 and holds a business degree from the University of Paris.

articles.title_orig: California’s economy continues to dominate — topping $4.5 T in economic output, and remains the world’s fourth largest economy
articles.title_zh: California’s economy continues to dominate — topping $4.5 T in economic output, and remains the world’s fourth largest economy
articles.content_orig:
What you need to know: New federal data shows California has surpassed $4.5 trillion in economic production, dominates across sectors, and is a leader in increasing wages and salaries.
SACRAMENTO — While Fox News pundits and politicians in Texas and Florida attack the tentpole of the U.S. economy, Governor Gavin Newsom today announced that California has reached a new milestone as the first U.S. state to surpass $4.5 trillion in economic output. Since 2019, California’s economy has increased by over half, at $1.58 trillion. Recent data also shows that California’s private sector alone has now crossed the $4 trillion mark for the first time.
California didn’t become a $4.5 trillion economy by accident. It happened because working people show up every day and build, grow, manufacture, invent, and move to power this state. Small businesses take the risks. Workers put in the hours. Entrepreneurs bet on the future. That’s the California story, and nobody does it at our scale.
Newly released data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis shows that California ranks first in economic output across almost every sector in 2025, including agriculture, manufacturing, technology, entertainment, healthcare, and wholesale trade. California’s economy grew by nearly $300 billion in the past year alone — the largest dollar gain of any state and $76 billion more than second-place taker-state Texas . These gains go deeper than just the GDP — on the individual level, total wages and salaries grew by 5.2%, and California is #1 for personal-income dollar gains this quarter. California also grew faster than Texas, Florida, and New York in 2025, expanding 3.5% after inflation.
California, the nation’s leader in manufacturing , also accounted for over 40% of total U.S. computer and electronics manufacturing and more than half of U.S. film and sound-recording output in 2025. The Golden State, home to 1.2 million manufacturing workers, pays more than $25,000 above the average non-farm wage, supporting families across the state.
The manufacturing jobs multiplier estimates that each manufacturing job supports three more in neighboring communities.
California manufacturers produced $391 billion in economic output in 2025, accounting for 9% of the state’s total GDP.
The state’s manufacturers exported $159 billion in goods in 2024.
Since 2021, California has invested over $215 million in over 675 contracts with employers to train over 194,000 workers in the manufacturing sector.
The Golden State represents only 11.5% of the U.S. population but is responsible for nearly 14% of U.S. GDP, 44% larger than taker-state Texas. California continues to lead the nation economically, outpacing all states and every developed nation , according to a Bloomberg analysis.
The state has more businesses than any other state, including Florida and Texas, supporting strong job creation and expanded economic opportunity for workers across the state. California is also home to more than 4.3 million small businesses , representing 99.8 percent of all businesses in the state and employing 7.6 million people .
As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California continues to lead the nation where it matters most — creating new businesses, attracting venture capital, driving technological innovation, expanding advanced manufacturing, growing high-tech industries, and producing more than any other state. In fact, the Golden State continues to be the #1 state for:
Governor Newsom recently signed new legislation to continue powering California’s economic engine:
✅ Making a major update to California’s antitrust and consumer protection laws. Clamping down on anti-competitive behavior , encouraging competition, and expanding opportunities for entrepreneurs and workers — including by creating new authority for the Attorney General and district attorneys to combat monopolistic behavior while also protecting small businesses.
✅ Helping retailers open and operate faster by allowing businesses undertaking certain tenant improvements to hire qualified architects or engineers to review and certify that building plans comply with life-safety, health, and building code requirements.
✅ Protecting small businesses from abusive financial practices by unscrupulous financing companies.
✅ Ensuring access to small business technical assistance by supporting providers who offer free or low-cost one-on-one, confidential consulting and training. This will help small businesses and entrepreneurs start, grow, expand, and create jobs in California.
✅ Cutting unnecessary red tape that has kept a lower-cost fuel option out of reach for California drivers. Removing a regulatory barrier to authorize the sale of E15 — gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol — in California.

articles.title_orig: New Orleans Saints legend Steve Gleason reflects on his 15-year ALS fight - ABC News
articles.title_zh: New Orleans Saints legend Steve Gleason reflects on his 15-year ALS fight - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
New Orleans Saints legend Steve Gleason is opening up about his 15-year journey with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, his place in the Saints' history books, and how his diagnosis brought him closer to other NFL players.
"Robin, I'm still here. That still surprises some people," Gleason told ABC News' Robin Roberts in an interview that aired Monday on " Good Morning America ." "It does not surprise me as much as it used to."
Gleason spoke with ABC News ahead of the Saints' Monday night game against the Atlanta Falcons, which marks the 20th anniversary of the Saints' return to the Superdome following Hurricane Katrina. During Monday's game, Gleason and former Saints teammate Curtis Deloatch will be honored as "Legends of the Game" in recognition of their roles in the Saints' 23-3 victory over the Atlanta Falcons on Sept. 25, 2006, the Saints' first home matchup at the Superdome since 2004, when it was damaged by Katrina.
Gleason was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, in 2011. ALS is a progressive nervous system disease that destroys nerve cells and causes motor function and muscle control loss, according to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
In people with ALS, the brain eventually "loses its ability to start and control voluntary movements such as walking, talking, chewing and other functions, as well as breathing," the agency states. While there are treatments approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration that may extend survival or slow functional decline, there is currently "no known treatment" that can stop or reverse the ALS' progression, according to NINDS.
"I cannot move, talk, or breathe on my own. Some days are brutal," Gleason said, speaking with Roberts. "And still, this is a miraculous, wonderful life. ... I wake up, I watch the sunrise, I am with [my wife] Michel, [kids] Rivers and Gray. I get to love this life and the people in it."
Today, Gleason said he uses his eyes to communicate and write with a special tablet. He also uses eye tape, often decorated by his children, to keep his eyebrows in position to work with his tablet.
"I live on a ventilator," Gleason explained. "I live knowing this breath is given to me by a machine, and this sentence is built letter by letter, and this moment with those I love is the whole point."
Gleason's role in the Saints' historic first home game back at the Superdome 20 years ago has served as a "lifeline" amid his journey with ALS, he said.
Gleason, a former safety for the Saints, cemented his place in team history during the 2006 game when he blocked a punt from Falcons punter Michael Koenen in the first quarter. Deloatch quickly recovered the ball, which had bounced backward into the end zone, giving the Saints their first touchdown of the game. The team has called that blocked punt touchdown "one of the most iconic moments in franchise history."
Gleason said he immediately recognized the impact of that moment and how much it meant for the city of New Orleans, which had been devastated by Katrina and was still rebuilding at the time. Later, however, he also came to realize its impact and importance in his own life, he said.
“If I do not block that punt, I am another former special teams player, a has-been football guy," Gleason said. "When the ALS came I probably fade away quietly and die anonymously."
He continued, "That play made me visible at the exact moment this city needed a symbol. Years later, that visibility became a lifeline."
Gleason said following his 2011 ALS diagnosis, the now-legendary on-field moment brought critical visibility and an elevated profile to Team Gleason, the nonprofit he founded in 2011 to advocate for, support and provide services to people living with ALS.
"The truth I have to live with is this: The same play that helped New Orleans breathe again is a big reason I'm still breathing now," he said.
On Monday night, Gleason will return to the Superdome alongside his family to celebrate that famous moment from 20 years ago.
"When I roll back into that stadium, I will not only be visiting a monument to 2006, I will be walking into a mirror, a place that learned how to rise," Gleason said. "I had to learn the same thing. Twenty years later, I can't wait to be in the room where that love still lives."
Gleason's diagnosis also led him to find strong community with other NFL players diagnosed with the disease, whom he affectionately refers to as his NFL "brothers."
" Chris Johnson is my NFL brother. Tim Shaw, O.J. Brigance, Eric Stevens, Steve Smith, others," Gleason said. "More importantly, they are my fellow humans. When ALS enters your life, it is a tsunami of emotions. I want everyone in their families to know they are not alone."
Gleason said he hasn't let ALS stop his creative endeavors either, which include a new album titled "Rebirth" that features his poetry and various New Orleans musicians.
"It's a love letter to the people and spirit of this wild place," Gleason said of the project. "Who better to bring that to life than the best musicians from right here in New Orleans? When we started reaching out around town, they kept saying yes. Their support has been one of the most meaningful parts of making this album for me."
In addition to Gleason's "Legends of the Game" honor, the Saints will honor Team Gleason during Monday night's game, making it "the beneficiary of the game's 50/50 raffle," the team said.
The NFL has also announced it will be donating $500,000 to research consortium Answer ALS' Champion Insights program, investigating ALS in professional football players, other high-performance athletes and military first responders.

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University protests escalate with spray paint and broken glass
articles.title_zh: Cornell University protests escalate with spray paint and broken glass
articles.content_orig:
Student activists defend their actions as nonviolent, saying ‘property damage is not violent, condoning rape is’
Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
Student activists vandalized a Cornell University administration building overnight in response to the university’s handling of gang-rape allegations in a high-profile case that has dominated national news.
Students smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall and painted messages on the walls at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported .
The messages, which read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED,” were written in red paint on the two walls surrounding the doors. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The actions were driven by a recent lawsuit alleging a 2024 fraternity-house gang rape and “in protest of the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”, according to a statement obtained by the student publication.
“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, said in a statement that the concerns of the community were being heard, but condemned damaging school property.
“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
The student activists defended their actions as nonviolent, in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”
Protests led by student activist groups are expected to take place on campus today.
Meanwhile, Cornell is under immense scrutiny after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.
According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.
Two of the Chi Phi fraternity members were expelled and a third, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reports . Two more were given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore, known in court papers as Jane Doe , and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit also claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.
Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
Additionally, in a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.

articles.title_orig: Philippines Accuses PLA of Unsafe Close Encounter Over South China Sea
articles.title_zh: Philippines Accuses PLA of Unsafe Close Encounter Over South China Sea
articles.content_orig:
Published
					Oct 5, 2026 5:47 PM        		by The Maritime Executive
The Philippine military says that a Chinese fighter made an unsafe close approach to a patrol aircraft near Scarborough Shoal, a contested reef west of Luzon in the South China Sea.
According to the AFP, a Philippine C-208 light patrol aircraft was conducting a flight near Scarborough on Saturday when it was approached by two Chinese military aircraft. One of the Chinese planes, a J-16 jet fighter, approached repeatedly and moved in too close for safe operation, the AFP claimed - including maneuvers in front and in back of the Philippine plane.
The C-208 is a small, unarmed prop plane used for maritime patrols in Philippine service. The Shenyang J-16 is a fourth-generation strike fighter derived from the design of the Soviet-era Su-27.
"This incident is part of a recurring pattern of unsafe and coercive behavior against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations," the AFP said in a statement. "The AFP will continue to conduct routine maritime and air patrols in the [western Philippine EEZ]."
The C-208 aircrew completed the mission and returned to base without incident, according to the AFP.
China claims the vast majority of the South China Sea as its own - including a large swathe of the Philippine EEZ - under its historically-derived "Nine Dash Line" claim and its more recent, geographically-based "Four Sha" straight-baseline theory. It seized control of Scarborough Shoal from Philippine forces in 2012 and has held it ever since. The Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in 2016 that these claims in the Philippine EEZ have no basis in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea; China refused to recognize the ruling and has continued to expand its presence in the region.
In accordance with China's views on sovereignty in the South China Sea, China's military and state media have an alternative account of Saturday's aircraft encounter. In China's view, PLA aircraft took action to expel a Philippine aircraft that "illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's [Scarborough Shoal]," 600 miles southeast of the Chinese mainland.
"[Scarborough Shoal] is China's inherent territory. The acts by the Philippine side seriously violate China’s sovereignty and are highly likely to cause unintended maritime and air incidents. We sternly warn the Philippine side to stop rights-violation and provocative acts immediately," a spokesman for China's Southern Theater Command said in a strongly-worded statement on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.title_zh: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.content_orig:
Photo by Judy Gallagher via Flickr, CC BY 2.0.
A Texas House Agriculture and Livestock Committee hearing on Friday, October 2 covered a range of topics affecting the state’s agricultural industry, including New World screwworm (NWS) — celebrating the state’s success in stifling its spread and warning about a surge in cases in Mexico.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) lists 52 cases of this flesh-eating livestock pest in the country since the first confirmation in June, 51 of which were found in Texas. One case appeared on the border between Texas and New Mexico, while one is fully within the latter state.
Based on both the USDA’s interactive NWS case dashboard and the Texas Animal Health Commission’s (TAHC) map of NWS zones, the majority of cases are located in West Texas, in counties including Val Verde, Edwards, and Crockett, while a significantly smaller portion is clustered near Roma.
While over a dozen cases occurred in July, August and September saw only four and three cases, respectively. So far in October, only one case has been confirmed — in a dog within Brewster County.
During the hearing, the committee heard testimony from various leaders in the state’s agricultural sector, who discussed a few interim charges assigned by Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R-Lubbock) for lawmakers to study ahead of the 90th Legislative Session.
The “invasive species” charge, which encompasses the focus on NWS while also addressing feral hogs and other parasites, reads : “Study the detection and management of invasive species and insects impacting Texas agriculture, including New World screwworm … Examine current prevention, response, and eradication efforts.”
Witnesses generally lauded Texas’ efforts alongside federal partners in preparing for the onslaught of NWS and in its response, while warning that the state is not quite out of the woods, as its neighbor Mexico continues to battle the infestation.
“Tremendous job we did in Texas getting through the summer. No question about it. It surprised the hell out of everybody,” said Thomas Lansford, representing the TAHC.
“But obviously, all hell is breaking loose in Mexico,” Lansford said.
The USDA is currently reporting 45,216 animal NWS cases through September 30 in Mexico, with 2,032 considered active cases.
Another TAHC representative, Dr. Lewis R. “Bud” Dinges, who is the Texas state veterinarian and the executive director of TAHC, similarly lauded the NWS response in Texas, saying, “None of the progress … would have been possible without the vigilance and participation of livestock producers, veterinarians, landowners, and other members of the public.”
But he added, “Our work will continue until the New World Screwworm is pushed out of Texas and back into Mexico. Until the pest is eradicated from Mexico, it will remain a risk to Texas and the United States.”
Since the first case was found in Zavala County in June, the USDA has released over 1.4 billion sterile flies as of October 1 to breed with the pests and prevent reproduction, a method that helped eliminate the NWS from the U.S. in 1966.
This method took center stage during the NWS discussion, as witnesses noted that the continued uptick in the pest’s presence in Mexico meant Texas could not yet rest easy, and that the outbreak would reduce Texas’ protection from the current sterile fly population concentrated in the Lone Star State.
Lansford continued in response to questions from Chairman Ryan Guillen (R-Rio Grande City) about the need for sterile flies to deal with outbreaks in other states: “With flies moving to the north and to the west, and Mexico … New Mexico is already in play … and then that brings Arizona and California into play.”
“If those states have cases, they’re going to take away what sterile flies we continue to disperse over our infested areas, and it's going to diminish what we have at our disposal,” he added.
The hearing concluded with general agreement among witnesses and lawmakers on the panel that while federal and local collaboration on the issue has proved successful, responders must remain vigilant as NWS spreads north and west through Mexico.
Mary Elise O'Bar is a reporter for The Texan , based in Southeast Texas. Her work has
been cited by The Hill, Newsweek, and congressional reporting. She
writes with a particular focus on social issues impacting  Texans,
and has spoken on various radio programs. She previously worked in
Washington, D.C. covering federal politics, and then in Austin
tracking the Texas Legislature. When she isn't reporting at local
events in Houston, she enjoys spending time with her husband,
reading, or exploring the great outdoors of Texas.

articles.title_orig: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.title_zh: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.content_orig:
A teenager has lost a hand in a grenade explosion as the return of school protests in France sparked clashes with police.
The 15-year-old was seriously injured in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Unverified police reports said that he had picked up a stun grenade.
France had said it would close up to 500 schools as demonstrations over understaffed and rundown schools entered a third week. Critics have called for the authorities to temper their response to the protests amid claims of disproportionate police force being used against minors.
The youth, injured near the Auguste-Behal vocational high school, was taken to hospital in Lille. His life is not in danger, according to Pas-de-Calais prefect Francois-Xavier Lauch.
A police union source reported that the student appeared to have picked up a rubber sting-ball or ”de-encirclement” grenade, fired by riot police, in an attempt to throw it back before it exploded in his hand, the AFP news agency reported.
Public prosecutors said investigators have yet to establish whether the teenager picked up the device or whether it landed on him.
They have referred the case to police internal affairs, which is now engaged in six investigations into serious injuries that have occurred during the student protests.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray described the teenager’s injury as “humanly dramatic” but said he would not comment further until the circumstances were established. He said 190 students had been injured since the protests began.
The Lens incident has added to scrutiny of police tactics during the demonstrations. Amnesty International France has criticised what it described as disproportionate police force against minors, saying it was alarmed by reports of students being hit with batons and subjected to tear gas and rubber-bullet fire known as LBDs.
The rights group said many of those taking part were minors under 18 and called on authorities to ensure policing methods were proportionate and compatible with France’s human rights obligations.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.
The Education Ministry said 589 schools had been disrupted on Monday, down from 735 on Friday, according to figures reported by Le Monde. Earlier estimates had suggested between 400 and 500 of France’s 3,700 high schools could be fully or partially closed.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.
Geffray said on Sunday that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked during the protests, with 78 teaching staff injured.
Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences.
“We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said.
“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.
Unrest and confrontations were reported in several cities on Monday. News channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school.
While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.
Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured.
Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while property damage costs are estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
Student unions have called for national demonstrations on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.content_orig:
Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.
Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.
Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.
The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr over how to classify measles-related mortality.
Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.
Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.
“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”
In New York state, governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.
Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.
In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.
Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.
According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s . That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.
The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .

articles.content_orig:
MESA, AZ (AZFamily) — Mesa Public Library goers can soon rock a new special edition library card for its 120th birthday.
The library announced Monday that it’s collaborating with Mesa’s own Jimmy Eat World on a library card that celebrates the band’s roots and also marks the 25th anniversary of their “Bleed American” album.
The Jimmy Eat World library card was designed to look like a vintage concert ticket, with nods to both the band and the library.
“We couldn’t be more excited to partner with the Mesa Public Library to design a Jimmy Eat World inspired library card to help celebrate their 120 th Anniversary,” the band said in a statement.
“We all grew up within a mile or so of the library in downtown Mesa and some of our earliest memories as kids were visits with our families or classmates to check out our favorite books. We believe so strongly in supporting ALL public libraries, but in particular Mesa Public Library because of all it has and continues to provide the community.”
The special edition library card will be available starting Sat., Oct. 10 at all Mesa library locations.
You can exchange your old library card for the Jimmy Eat World design for free.
The library will be celebrating its 120th anniversary at the Main Library location on Oct. 10 from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.
The Gateway Library, which opened earlier this year in Mesa, was recently named one of the best in the world , winning the 2026 IFLA/James Bennett Public Library of the Year Award.

articles.title_orig: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.title_zh: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday called China “an important neighbor” and pledged continued dialogue with Beijing amid strained ties over her previous comments on Taiwan.
“China is an important neighbor, and our relationship has been built over many years despite existing challenges,” Takaichi said in a policy speech to parliament, according to the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office.
“We will comprehensively advance a ‘mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests,’” she added.
Diplomatic relations between Japan and China have deteriorated significantly since Takaichi said in November that Tokyo could intervene if Taiwan were attacked, despite Beijing saying that the island is part of its territory.
Takaichi said Japan would clearly state its positions on issues in the East and South China seas, Chinese military activity around Japan, “coercive measures,” the safety of Japanese nationals and human rights concerns.
“We will maintain dialogue on shared challenges, protect Japan’s national interests and work toward a constructive and stable relationship,” she added.
Takaichi’s statement came a week after former Japanese Foreign Minister Takeshi Iwaya visited Beijing and met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Wang urged Takaichi to “correct” her remarks on Taiwan and said bilateral relations needed to be normalized.
Relations between Japan and China have deteriorated significantly since Takaichi said in November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise collective self-defense.

articles.title_orig: SSPI Explores US-China Space Law, Export Controls, and Cross-Border Regulatory Frameworks
articles.title_zh: SSPI Explores US-China Space Law, Export Controls, and Cross-Border Regulatory Frameworks
articles.content_orig:
On October 5, 2026, Space & Satellite Professionals International (SSPI) released Episode 5 of its Collateral Risk podcast series, examining the legal, regulatory, and policy friction impacting cross-border commercial space ventures between the United States and China.
Hosted by SSPI Executive Director Tamara Bond-Williams, the episode features a discussion with Fuhua Ni, Founding and Managing Partner of Shanghai Zenith Law Firm, focusing on navigating export controls and establishing formal industry channels between regional space ecosystems.
China’s commercial space sector has expanded rapidly following initial market liberalization policy shifts in 2014, yet its domestic legal and regulatory infrastructure remains distributed across multiple government agencies and regional jurisdictions. During the discussion, Ni detailed how international commercial law practices interface with complex space law structures, highlighting the operational constraints imposed by trade compliance regimes including the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), Export Administration Regulations (EAR), and the Congressional Wolf Amendment.
The episode also evaluates a proposed Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) report assessing potential avenues for bilateral US–China space cooperation, alongside the challenges of managing dual-use technologies where commercial systems support national security functions.
The broadcast forms part of SSPI’s broader The Defense of Space sector campaign, launched alongside the Collateral Risk podcast series to address the strategic exposure created as military operations integrate commercial low Earth orbit (LEO) constellations. The initiative investigates legal frameworks governing satellite targeting during conflict, the extent of US commitments to defend commercial space infrastructure, and operational implications surrounding NATO’s Article 5 space declarations.
To build durable cross-border industry relationships and facilitate regulatory dialogue, Ni is currently leading the preparatory group to establish an official SSPI China chapter. The professional network aims to provide commercial space operators, legal professionals, and policy analysts with a structured forum to address emerging space governance, mediation, and arbitration protocols as commercial space assets become increasingly central to global commerce and national security architectures.
