British Airways has today unveiled new cabins arriving on its retrofitted A380s, marking a major milestone in one of the most extensive cabin refurbishment programmes ever undertaken by an airline.
From nose to tail, customers will experience a transformed A380 aircraft, featuring redesigned interiors, new seats in every cabin and upgrades to the onboard experience, all designed to deliver greater comfort and a more premium end-to-end journey at 35,000ft.
The first completed A380 is expected to enter service in the coming months, marking the start of a fleet-wide transformation and forming part of the airline's wider investment in the customer experience.
Sean Doyle, Chairman and CEO at British Airways, said: "This is a major milestone for British Airways and the future of our A380 fleet, marking one of the most significant transformations we’ve ever undertaken on any aircraft.
‘We've completely reimagined the customer experience, introducing new and updated seats in every cabin, all carefully considered to deliver greater comfort and an elevated customer experience.
‘At the heart of the transformation is our brand-new First suite, but this investment goes far beyond a single cabin. From redesigned interiors and upgraded dining to new amenities and service delivery, every detail has been thoughtfully designed with our customers front and centre, helping them to have a more seamless and memorable experience when they fly with us."
Customers travelling in Club World (business class), World Traveller Plus (premium economy) and World Traveller (economy) will benefit from brand-new seats and upgraded cabin interiors. Thoughtfully redesigned with customer comfort in mind, the airline’s herringbone design features throughout the cabins.
Every part of the aircraft has been refined, including galleys and stairways bringing a new look and feel to every space on board.
From seat details to galley finishes, the new interiors create a clear identity throughout the aircraft, building on the design concept first introduced to the airline's short-haul fleet in 2024 and now shaping the future of its long-haul cabins.
New cabins with added comfort in mind
World Traveller and World Traveller Plus
Customers in World Traveller (economy) will enjoy a refreshed experience, including larger entertainment screens, wider seats and upgraded bedding. The relaxing new pillows feature a contemporary herringbone pattern and additional filling for added comfort and support. Plusher blankets, designed for added warmth and comfort have also been introduced in British Airways’ signature blue with red Speedmarque detailing.
Customers travelling in World Traveller Plus (premium economy) will also benefit from a host of improvements designed to make every journey more comfortable and relaxing. Seats will feature larger in-flight entertainment screens and privacy wings, alongside brand-new bedding and pillows helping customers arrive feeling rested and refreshed.
Customers travelling in World Traveller Plus will receive a new reusable amenity kit, designed as a tote bag for onward travel and featuring a Dr.PAWPAW moisturising balm and travel essentials, including a dental kit, socks and eye mask*.
The A380 will feature an evolution of British Airways’ Club Suite (business class) showcasing a refreshed design with a contemporary colour palette inspired by the airline’s blue, red and cream accents. Shaped by customer feedback, the suite includes added storage, improved functionality and carefully considered features designed to make every journey more comfortable and intuitive.
The aircraft will feature the world’s largest business class cabin, including 106 Club Suite seats across the full upper deck. Spanning four distinct cabin zones, the carefully designed space will offer a more intimate feel, complemented by dedicated dwell areas, Club Kitchens and reimagined galley spaces that encourage customers to move freely and relax throughout the flight.
Customers travelling in Club World will also enjoy the airline’s latest amenity kits, available in four unique designs created by British artists, powered by art platform, Rise Art, and stocked with exclusive products from luxury British wellness brand, anatomē.
A defining feature of the retrofit is British Airways' new First suite, combining ultimate comfort and privacy with considered touches to create an elegant space for customers to relax and unwind.
Designed to evoke a modern luxury hotel feel, the airline’s First cabin combines home comforts with thoughtful British touches at 35,000ft. The seat has been brought to life by expert designers and world-class manufacturers from across Great Britain and Ireland.
For customers travelling together in the centre seats, the divider opens to create a shared lounge, while stowable tables allow them to enjoy ‘buddy dining’ with their travel companion.
British Airways has partnered with luxury British heritage house, Swaine, to create a bespoke unisex First amenity kit inspired by the heritage suitcases carried by early air travellers, available on board from 6 October**.
Available in two colours, royal blue and cream, the kit contains a selection of skincare products from Wildsmith, a high-performance skincare brand that supports skin health and wellbeing. The kit will include a bespoke Circadian Rhythm collection aimed at supporting hydration and comfort from day into night.
The products include a face mist, hand and body lotion, ceramide multi-balm, lip balm, face cream, and an overnight mask, all carefully curated to support hydration and rest at altitude.
Hotel-quality sleep at 35,000ft
Customers in First can relax under a brand-new woven day blanket, featuring an elegant herringbone design. The new blanket will be complemented by a navy-blue cushion with subtle detailing. The airline’s bespoke tartan will also feature on the new cool-touch fabric navy sleepwear, complemented by slippers, all available on board from 1 October.
When it's time to sleep, crew will prepare the suite with a luxury mattress, lightweight cotton duvet and newly designed pillow, carefully developed to offer the ideal balance of softness and support, helping customers secure a great night’s sleep and arrive feeling refreshed at their destination.
Restaurant dining in the sky
The airline’s refreshed First dining service offers customers greater choice, using fresh flavours and new dishes that reflect the best of British produce.
The new dining experience will be available across the airline’s entire long-haul fleet from 1 October. A new ‘From the Grill’ concept means customers can create their preferred meal from a selection of premium proteins including British roast rack of lamb, grilled salmon, sides and sauces, as well as a selection of Signature Mains for a more personalised dining experience.
For added convenience, a bespoke mini bar has been integrated into the new First seat, giving customers easy access to popular refreshments throughout the flight, including a selection of premium snacks and still and sparkling water.
The new dining experience is complemented by contemporary stoneware and fine bone china, bringing a refined, restaurant-inspired feel to every course. A dedicated beverage menu features premium Champagne such as Bollinger La Grande Année, alongside a curated gin selection, such as Classic Gin Tonic, Rosemary & Orange, Spanish Flair as well as 0.0% Gin & Tonic. Customers can also enjoy a refreshing Showerings triple vintage cider as refined alternative to wine.
Every detail has been carefully considered, from cutlery designed by Studio William to wine glasses developed in collaboration with Richard Brendon and internationally renowned wine expert, Jancis Robinson.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock climbs to highest since June, returning Musk to trillionaire status
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares rose almost 8% on Monday, reaching their highest since mid-June, shortly after Elon Musk's company held its record initial public offering . With the rally, Musk is once again a trillionaire.
The jump followed a Sunday note from Morgan Stanley analysts, who called SpaceX "cheap" at today's prices, and highlighted "future AI product releases, Starship progress, and additional neocloud contracts." They recommend buying the stock and have a $300 price target, representing an increase of about 75% from Monday's $171.09 close.
Late last week SpaceX conducted multiple historic flights in a single day, including sending a crewed mission for NASA to the International Space Station, and a separate launch of Google AI chips into orbit.
The Morgan Stanley analysts suggested investors buy SpaceX shares before the company's next planned test flight for its massive Starship rocket, and ahead of its third-quarter earnings report expected in late October.
Starship is SpaceX's next-generation spacecraft, the largest rocket ever built, and is designed to be fully reusable with both its upper stage and booster able to land safely back on Earth. The system is expected to supercharge SpaceX's business, bringing the company's Starlink satellites into orbit, as well as cargo and crews from other companies and agencies.
Should SpaceX attempt a Starship upper stage ship catch in its next test flight, that could be "the biggest positive catalyst since the IPO," the analysts wrote. In prior test flights, the Starship upper stage has made splash downs in the ocean, but hasn't been proven reusable.
SpaceX is also getting a boost from its artificial intelligence business, which it gained through the acquisition of Musk's xAI last year and expanded through the recent acquisition of Cursor. While the company's homegrown Grok model hasn't taken off compared to leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, SpaceX is generating hefty revenue by renting out capacity to the likes of Google and Anthropic.
Musk has the benefit of close ties to the Trump administration.
On Wednesday, the Pentagon appointed Musk as co-lead of Project Meridian , an initiative that involves identifying weapons, technologies and military capabilities the U.S. may need in future wars. SpaceX makes a large chunk of its revenue from the U.S. government and increasingly from defense contracts,  earning over $12.7 billion to date from its work with the Defense Department, according to FedScout.
Musk said over the weekend he will be renaming SpaceX's AI division, known as SpaceXAI, as SpaceXSI, embracing President Donald Trump's new branding.
As his company's stock soared on Monday, Musk was notably absent from a New York City Council hearing , where city officials grilled AI leaders and researchers about how the technology should be regulated. Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta were in attendance to testify.
Councilmember Shekar Krishnan noted, "AI has taken over our economy, inflated valuations, stealing our public land for data centers, and increasing the net worth of AI CEOs like Elon Musk, who became our first ever trillionaire."
According to Forbes' real-time billionaires list , Musk is currently worth $1.03 trillion, factoring in his holdings in Tesla and SpaceX.
SpaceX went public on June 12, and jumped to a record close of $201.80 on June 16. The shares started trending lower soon thereafter, bottoming in early August. They've since climbed about 58%.
SpaceX didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.title_zh: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.content_orig:
The following story originally appeared on the website for the William & Mary College of Arts & Sciences. – Ed.
“When they say, ‘Houston, we have a problem’ in movies, they are hailing mission control. However, when mission control has problems, they contact us,” said Elisa Leal Acevedo M.S. ’25, an engineer in NASA’s Mission Evaluation Room (MER) during the Artemis II mission.
The MER monitors all data coming in from the Orion spacecraft, searching for anomalies. Acevedo, who graduated from William & Mary with a master’s degree in computational operations research, utilized her operations skills to assist the Artemis II mission earlier this year.
The Computational and Applied Mathematics master’s degree with a Concentration in Operations Research (CAM-COR) is an updated name for a long-standing program at W&M. The new program, which took effect in August 2026, is also offered as a Bachelor’s-to-Master’s Accelerated Pathway (BMAP) for W&M undergraduates.
The core of the program consists of courses in operations research, mathematical modeling for random processes, probability and optimization. These theories are correlated to real-world business and safety challenges, such as optimal traffic light timing and customer queuing.
The program is led by seven distinguished professors, who come from a range of backgrounds that inform their respective classes and research, helping students connect mathematical modeling with real-world decision-making.
Graduates apply their degree in an array of fields. Recent CAM-COR graduate Acevedo worked six shifts in NASA’s MER in Houston for the Artemis II mission this past year. In her role as a subject matter expert on the Flight Software Console team, Acevedo monitored Orion’s Environmental Control and Life Support Subsystem’s software, making sure it was operating as expected in real time.
“My COR degree helped me apply the decision-making skills I developed in the program when encountering anomalies in the MER,” Acevedo said. These skills allowed her to quickly assess courses of action, analyze probability of recurrence and perform risk analysis. She also optimized limited spacecraft resources such as bandwidth allocations, considering operational constraints at the same time.
“Post-mission, I am now exploring software reliability methods that can be applied to the flight software on future missions,” she said.
While Acevedo’s work focuses on the depths of space, a current student is specializing in defense research. Anne Kredell ‘26 first took CAM-COR classes as an undergraduate at W&M and is now a master’s student in the program. She applied her studies this past summer as an intern for the Naval Information Warfare Center in San Diego, where she focused on radio frequency machine learning.
Though this was a new area for Kredell, she was able to adapt and tackle the project. “My COR coursework prepared me to approach this challenge, and my mathematical skills allowed me to suceed,” Kredell said. “The technical skills and critical-thinking abilities I developed in those classes were integral to my success this past summer.”
Faculty in the program put the versatility of a CAM-COR degree on display through their diverse professional and research experiences, showcasing the breadth of opportunities the degree can support. For example, adjunct professor Dave Williams is a former chief operating officer of the U.S. Postal Service, while Rex Kincaid, Chancellor Professor of Mathematics, is conducting research in the marine science world. Kincaid is developing optimization models to determine the best locations to build new oyster reefs in the Chesapeake Bay.
Even closer to campus than the Chesapeake Bay, Larry Leemis, a professor for the COR program since 1993, conducts research for Colonial Williamsburg. In the 1990s, he worked to determine the optimal number of weekly tourist guides to print. Three decades later, Leemis is researching new topics for the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation, such as optimizing maintenance routines for equipment.
These professors, through studying a range of applications of operations research, utilize their experience to encourage students to find the next problem that can be solved with mathematical modeling.
After a fruitful internship, Kredell is eager to continue working in operations research, specifically within the defense sector, post-graduation. “This degree prepares me for a wide array of careers,” she said. “Beyond the specific technical tools I am learning, the program is teaching me how to approach varying problems systemically and how to communicate my findings clearly.”
From Chesapeake Bay oyster health to NASA lunar missions, the CAM-COR master’s degree program continues its legacy of instilling real-world problem-solving skills, preparing students to optimize systems across industries.
Applications for spring admission to the program are open until Oct. 15 .
Rebecca Ries '27, College of Arts & Sciences

articles.title_orig: Karl Deisseroth wins Nobel Prize
articles.title_zh: Karl Deisseroth wins Nobel Prize
articles.content_orig:
A Stanford University professor was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for pioneering work that helped give scientists an unprecedented way to control and study nerve cells using light.
Karl Deisseroth, a professor of Bioengineering and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at Stanford and an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, shares the prize with Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. In a statement on Monday, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, Sweden, cited the three scientists “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.”
The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor or around $1.2 million, will be divided equally among the three laureates.
Their work transformed a biological curiosity found in a single-celled alga into a powerful tool for neuroscience, according to the Nobel Foundation. Hegemann and Nagel discovered a protein called channelrhodopsin in Chlamydomonas, an alga that uses light to navigate. When exposed to blue light, the protein opens a channel that allows charged ions to flow through the cell, producing an electrical impulse.
Later, Deisseroth saw a way to use that mechanism to investigate the brain. He introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into rat nerve cells, making the cells responsive to blue light. In 2005, he published the breakthrough showing that light could be used to trigger nerve signals.
Two years later, he demonstrated that the technique could control nerve cells in the brains of living mice. The approach became known as optogenetics.
Unlike many earlier methods for studying the brain, optogenetics allows researchers to manipulate particular groups of nerve cells with precise timing. Deisseroth’s discovery has helped scientists investigate neural circuits involved in memories, emotions and behavior — including circuits relevant to neurological and psychiatric disorders, the Nobel Foundation said.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.
Background Deisseroth was born on Nov. 18, 1971, in Boston, Massachusetts, according to the university website.
He earned his undergraduate degree in biochemical sciences from Harvard, graduating summa cum laude, before earning his Ph.D. in neuroscience and M.D. from Stanford. He completed medical internship and adult psychiatry residency training at Stanford and is board-certified in psychiatry by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology.
According to the Stanford University website, he remains a practicing psychiatrist at the educational institution, where he specializes in affective disorders and autism spectrum disorder and uses both medication and neural stimulation in treating patients.

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump’s safety pact
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump’s safety pact
articles.content_orig:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.
During Politico’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.
The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.
Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .
In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.
Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.
In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.
Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too.
“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.
The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead.
“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

articles.title_orig: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.title_zh: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.content_orig:
The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.
The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Key details remain unknown, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people that came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media.
“Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine.
Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.”
“We need to understand that now,” he added.
The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is.
Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics.
It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization . All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body.
Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious.
Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said.
Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood.
Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes.
The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.”
It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO.
Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said.
“It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said.
Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet.
“It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said.
While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest.
“It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said.
It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm.
Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici.
People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Health care workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure.
“We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said.
Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague.
“This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said.
Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.”
Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.”
“The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said.
About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC . Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas.
Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen.
Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague .
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_orig: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.title_zh: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

articles.title_orig: Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27
articles.title_zh: Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27
articles.content_orig:
A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk , even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27″ in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page . They said that Apple’s Intelligence models take up “about 12GB,” but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.
RemoveMacAI “turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again. Dictation still works because it’s a separate setting,” the developer said in a Reddit post first spotted by MacRumors .
On Reddit, RemoveMacAI’s developer said the tool is open source and further explained how it works:
It uses a configuration profile you approve in System Settings plus Apple’s own asset service, so [ System Integrity Protection ] stays on and nothing in /System gets touched directly. removemacai revert removes the profile, and macOS downloads the models again when you turn a feature back on.
The dev also said you can remove only the Apple Intelligence features you don’t want and keep the others.
Some users on Reddit have reported that the tool works, and it has 1,700 stars on GitHub as of this writing.
Interest in RemoveMacAI demonstrates the aversion that some users have to some or all of Apple Intelligence’s features, despite growing focus from Apple on AI-driven device and software upgrades in its computers and other devices .
“Reminds me of all the de-crufting you’ve always needed to do when you install Windows. Looks like we’ve gotten to the point on macOS too, where you need to run third-party scripts on a new OS installation to gain back control of your system resources and remove unwanted crapware,” a Hacker News user wrote in response to RemoveMacAI.
Although many users are happy to leverage Apple Intelligence in their gadgets, RemoveMacAI is a simple way for the rest to regain control over Apple Intelligence’s presence on their computers that Apple previously offered.

articles.title_orig: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
Preschoolers at The Goddard School in Plymouth recently got a hands-on introduction to broadcast journalism during a special visit from CCX News anchor Emily Haugen in honor of World News Day.
During the visit, the young students stepped behind the anchor desk, practiced using real microphones and tried their hand at interviewing. The interactive session gave them a taste of how news reporting works, featuring lighthearted conversations about their favorite colors, sports and pets at home.
“So I just asked all of them what their favorite color is, so I’ll ask that to you, too,” Haugen asked one student during a practice interview. “What is your favorite color?”
“Purple!” the student replied.
“Why is purple your favorite color?”
The activity aligns directly with the school’s focus on inquiry-based learning, according to school owner Anthony Miller.
“I think any time you can add curiosity to anything, kids learn well with that,” Miller said.
The Goddard School frequently hosts visitors from various professional backgrounds to introduce students to different career paths and foster early curiosity about the world around them.

articles.title_orig: California boy, 13, left in grim condition after coming down with rare disease
articles.title_zh: California boy, 13, left in grim condition after coming down with rare disease
articles.content_orig:
A California boy who was once a healthy, soccer-loving teenager is now fighting to regain the use of his legs after a seemingly harmless mosquito bite triggered a devastating medical nightmare.
Joseph Vasquez, 13, of Long Beach, has been bedridden at Children's Hospital Los Angeles for three weeks after contracting West Nile virus and developing transverse myelitis, a rare neurological condition that causes severe inflammation of the spinal cord, according to a GoFundMe launched by his family.
The frightening ordeal began with what appeared to be ordinary mosquito bites but quickly spiraled into a life-altering medical crisis.
Joseph Vasquez, a 13-year-old boy from Long Beach, remains hospitalized at Children's Hospital Los Angeles. Gofundme
Joseph initially developed a full-body rash, mild headache, leg pain and low-grade fever. But his symptoms rapidly worsened, eventually leaving him unable to move either leg.
The teen also experienced excruciating abdominal pain, a stiff neck and loss of bladder and bowel control as his condition deteriorated.
Doctors initially diagnosed Joseph with transverse myelitis and began treating him with steroids. After days in intensive care and extensive testing, they determined that West Nile virus was behind the devastating complications.
Now, the boy who once spent his days playing soccer, hanging out with his cousins and cheering on the Dodgers, Raiders and Lakers is facing an uncertain road to recovery.
"Today, Joseph is facing challenges no 13-year-old should ever have to face," his family wrote on the fundraiser. "He has lost the use of his legs, loss of bladder and bowel control, and is in excruciating nerve pain from the lower back down to his feet."
Joseph Vasquez has been diagnosed with transverse myelitis, a rare neurological condition linked to the West Nile virus. Courtesy of the Vasques Family
The family said doctors have warned that Joseph's condition is extraordinarily rare, with limited research available to predict how his recovery might unfold.
His mother, Maria Salazar, a widowed mother of three, has remained at his bedside around the clock. But the heartbreaking ordeal has also created a financial crisis for the family.
As the household's sole provider, Salazar has been unable to work while caring for her hospitalized son, prompting relatives to seek donations for living expenses, medical bills, transportation and rehabilitation.
"We never imagined that something that began with what seemed like minor symptoms could change Joseph's life so quickly," the family wrote.
Joseph Vasquez in happier times with his family. Gofundme
Joseph's terrifying case comes as Los Angeles County grapples with an alarming surge in West Nile infections.
The county's Department of Public Health has reported 100 infections and five deaths this year, the highest number of cases recorded this early in mosquito season in nearly a decade.
Nearly all reported cases this year have involved severe illness, with most patients requiring hospitalization, although health officials noted that milder infections frequently go undiagnosed.
"West Nile virus can cause serious illness, and the number of severe cases and deaths we are seeing this year is concerning," Los Angeles County Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis warned.
The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health has reported 100 infections and five deaths this year, the highest number of cases recorded this early in mosquito season in nearly a decade. Getty Images
Most people infected with West Nile virus experience no symptoms, while approximately one in five develops fever, headaches, body aches or a rash.
However, roughly one in 150 infected people develops a severe illness, potentially involving the brain or spinal cord and causing paralysis.
There is no vaccine or specific treatment for the virus.
With peak mosquito season stretching from June through November, health officials are urging residents to use insect repellent, eliminate standing water and repair damaged window screens.
Meanwhile, Joseph's family is pleading for prayers and support as the teenager faces an uncertain future.
"We are holding onto hope knowing that Joseph still has a long road ahead of him," his family wrote.

articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.content_orig:
About / Offices / Vocations
About / Offices / Vocations
Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_orig: Hofstadter’s butterfly turns 50: a fractal hiding in quantum matter
articles.title_zh: Hofstadter’s butterfly turns 50: a fractal hiding in quantum matter
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Indu Satija celebrates the 50th anniversary of the publication of Douglas Hofstadter’s eponymous, iconic butterfly and explains its enduring, magnetic appeal
In the mid-1970s a graduate student wrestling with a deceptively simple quantum problem uncovered one of the most haunting images in modern physics. The pattern seemed almost impossibly intricate: delicate wings assembled from infinitely nested bands and gaps, a self-similar pattern born from the motion of electrons in a crystal under a magnetic field. First published in 1976 ( Phys. Rev. B 14 2239 ), it came to be known as Hofstadter’s butterfly, after its discoverer Douglas Hofstadter .
Half a century later, the butterfly has not faded into scientific nostalgia. If anything, it has become even more important – reappearing in new materials, new experiments and in places no-one imagined when it was first plotted. Recent research by Kazuki Ikeda from the University of Massachusetts and Yaron Oz at Stony Brook University suggests that related patterns may even surface in the physics of black holes ( J. High Energy Phys. 2026 38 ).
Each new realization adds another chapter to a story that is not really about a single graph, or even a single discovery, but about the unity of patterns across the physical world. A structure first seen in a simple model has become a symbol of how richness can emerge from basic rules, how beauty can arise from constraint, and how the quantum world still harbours forms strange enough to surprise us.
What makes Hofstadter’s butterfly so compelling is the remarkable story of its birth and, more importantly, how far it has travelled from its original birthplace. Like many scientific breakthroughs, its discovery was fairly obscure initially and owed a great deal to luck. In 1974 Hofstadter – son of the 1961 Nobel-prize-winning nuclear physicist Robert Hofstadter – had just dropped out of graduate school at Stanford University in the US and was “in despair” according to friend and physicist Francisco Claro .
Having just completed a PhD with the renowned solid-state physicist Gregory Wannier at the University of Oregon, Claro suggested that Hofstadter should approach Wannier as well. As it happened, Wannier had been struggling with a problem that had puzzled him for years: he could not obtain an analytical solution to Harper’s equation , which describes the motion of electrons on a 2D crystal lattice subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field.
Named after P G Harper , who was a graduate student of Rudolf Peierls at the University of Birmingham, UK, this classic “magnetic problem” displayed a mysterious sensitivity to whether the magnetic flux was a rational or irrational number. It was a feature that immediately captured Hofstadter’s imagination and, with the rational–irrational dichotomy echoing in his mind, Hofstadter began his PhD studies at Oregon by immersing himself in solving the problem.
But he soon found himself equally stuck. Frustrated by the analytical approaches often discussed at the time, he pursued a different path: numerical computation. Using a programmable Hewlett Packard desktop calculator that by today’s standards looks laughably primitive, he displayed the numerical solutions graphically as the energy of electrons versus magnetic flux Φ per unit cell of the lattice. At that moment, he became convinced that he had uncovered the true structure of the problem. “All at once my eyes were opened,” Hofstadter recalls.
What he found was a complex recursive shape (or fractal in today’s terminology) hidden within the energy spectrum of electrons in a magnetic field. Resembling a butterfly, Hofstadter brought his hand-plotted diagram, which he codenamed “Gplot”, to Wannier, who was not impressed. According to Hofstadter, Wannier dismissed the result as “numerology” and even threatened to withdraw the PhD student’s funding.
But after nearly a year, Wannier came to recognize the validity and significance of Hofstadter’s work, ultimately awarding Hofstadter his PhD and accepting the butterfly as a legitimate description of the energy spectrum of electrons moving on a 2D lattice in a magnetic field. Wannier even added to the butterfly’s story with a paper titled “A result not dependent on rationality for Bloch electrons in a magnetic field ( Phys. Status Solidi b 88 757 ). This work, along with further studies with Claro, introduced a set of integers uniquely labelling every gap in the graph, providing a simplified description of the spectrum ( Phys. Rev. B 19 6068 ).
Ruby celebration Douglas Hofstadter (right) pictured in 2016 with colleagues Indu Satija (centre) and Francisco Claro (left) all wearing T-shirts emblazoned with Hofstadter’s butterfly to celebrate its 40th anniversary. (Courtesy: Indu Satija)
Born in 1945, Douglas Hofstadter discovered his eponymous butterfly while a PhD student at the University of Oregon in 1975, using computational modelling to make his breakthrough (see main text). Four years later Hofstadter published his Pulitzer-prize-winning popular-science book Gödel, Escher, Bach , which tackles cognition, mathematics and symmetry.
Currently a professor of cognitive science and comparative literature at Indiana University in Bloomington, US, Hofstadter is still active as a researcher and wrote a follow-up book I Am a Strange Loop in 2007. On the golden jubilee of the now-famous butterfly named after him, Hofstadter provided the following comment to Physics World .
“This graph was first computed using a programmable desktop calculator and was first plotted by hand using coloured felt-tip pens. I was just extremely relieved that by showing that my ‘Gplot’ graph was made of distorted copies of itself, I would at last be able to get a PhD thesis. I had no idea that Gplot would go on to become well known as the Hofstadter butterfly, and that variations on the theme would proliferate like wildfire over the coming decades.”
“As the years have gone by,” he continues, “articles about Hofstadter’s butterfly have grown more and more numerous and harder and harder for me to follow. For better or for worse, these theories are all way beyond me, but remembering the first wingbeats of the butterfly’s flight cheers me up.”
Hofstadter’s butterfly is more than a beautiful graph. It is a map of what happens when quantum particles are caught between two competing kinds of order: the regular periodicity of a crystal lattice and the circular orbits of a magnetic field. When these two scales contend with one another, the energy spectrum does something extraordinary. Instead of varying smoothly, it fragments into a hierarchy of allowed and forbidden energies, referred to as bands and gaps, respectively.
Zoom in on one region and new structures emerge. Zoom in again and the pattern repeats, endlessly varied yet ruled by strict mathematical order. It is one of the rare instances in which fractal geometry appears not only in abstract mathematics or artistic imagination, but in the measurable behaviour of matter itself.
The deep connection between this theoretical pattern and real-world matter became clear through an exotic quantum phenomenon known as the integer quantum Hall effect . It was discovered experimentally by Klaus von Klitzing at the Max Planck Institute for Solid-State Physics in 1980 – a breakthrough that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics five years later.
The classical Hall effect is what happens when a voltage is produced in a bulk conductor at right angles to an applied magnetic field. Similarly, the quantum Hall effect is the appearance of a voltage across opposite faces of a thin 2D semiconductor when a current is passed along the plane of the material and a magnetic field applied perpendicularly it. But there is one big difference in the quantum version.

articles.title_orig: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
articles.title_zh: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
articles.content_orig:
Police and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-Hammami
Investigators believe the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.
The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe.
Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.
Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.
Israeli media have quoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near ⁠Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar , said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.
In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia , where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.
The investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are examining reports that the co-pilot studied in both nations about 10 years ago.
Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, but left the airline after being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.
Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.
A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.
Netanyahu has claimed Hammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.
Nine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.
An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.
“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.
“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, a co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.
Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.
Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.
The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.
Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”

articles.title_orig: SoCal heat wave shatters multiple records, and the misery is far from over
articles.title_zh: SoCal heat wave shatters multiple records, and the misery is far from over
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Southern California has seen some toasty Octobers, but this year’s start to the fall season has been marked by a persistent heat wave that’s shattered records and ushered in an unprecedented streak of 100-degree days.
The extreme heat is driven by a persistent high pressure ridge that has parked over the region causing sinking warming air with very little overnight relief. That is paired with down-sloping winds and uncharacteristically warm ocean temperatures — driven in part by an El Niño that has reduced Southern California’s sea breeze, frequently known as its natural air conditioning.
“We’re going on Day 4 of this really significant heat wave and we still have several more days of heat,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. “We do have heat events in October, but this streak of 100-plus days is definitely starting to become pretty notable.”
The average number of 100-degree days in downtown Los Angeles in a typical October has been closer to zero than one since the weather service began keeping records in the late 1800s. This month, downtown is on a four-day consecutive streak of temperatures 100 degrees or higher — the longest consecutive stretch in October since records began.
Downtown is currently tied for the most 100-degree-plus days in October with 1958 and 1971, but could surpass those years if the mercury hits 100 degrees Tuesday, according to the weather service.
“If we get another one tomorrow, then we would be at the most 100-degree-plus days in October in downtown L.A. ever,” Schoenfeld said.
Saturday’s game started 45 minutes after the National Weather Service issued an extreme heat warning as the temperature reached 100 degrees at first pitch at Dodger Stadium.
The current heat wave already has broken daily heat records across the Southland.
Downtown Los Angeles broke a daily heat record Monday with the mercury reaching 104 degrees, shattering the previous record of 101 set in 1954 and tied in 1971.
The Burbank Airport hit 101 degrees Sunday, breaking the previous record of 100 set in 1964. Camarillo hit 99 degrees, inching past the previous record of 98 set in 1953. And Oxnard hit 99 degrees Sunday, shattering the daily record of 94 set in 2023.
In Orange County, Anaheim hit 101 degrees Sunday, blowing past the 98-degree record set in 2020.
San Diego hit 100 degrees, toppling a record of 97 set in 1987. The Oceanside Harbor registered 98 on Sunday, toppling the record of 97 set in 1953. And Ramona hit 101, just past the record of 100 set in 1987.
“It’s going to be pretty darn warm,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said of this week during a recent briefing on his Weather West channel.
Temperatures between 15 and 22 degrees above normal are expected to persist through Thursday. Highs along the coasts and valleys will be in the 90s up to the low 100s in the coming days. Even the beaches will provide little relief, with temperatures in the upper 80s.
The ocean is expected to bring its own dangers beginning Tuesday with elevated morning and evening tides and elevated surf as a result of Hurricane Rachel, located several hundred miles off the coast of Baja California with sustained winds of up to 85 mph.
The weather service is warning of dangerous rip currents and elevated surf of 3 to 6 feet on Catalina and Santa Barbara Islands as well as at Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches. The most susceptible areas will be Long Beach and the Avalon Harbor on Tuesday and Wednesday and then Malibu through Ventura County from Wednesday through Friday.
“Moderate flooding of sea water is a possibility over some vulnerable low-lying coastal areas, especially around the morning and evening high tides, including over beach parking lots, bike paths, and harbor walkways. Moderate beach erosion is possible to likely,” according to the weather service.
And those looking for relief won’t find it overnight.
It’ll still be warm after dark too, forecasters say, with the mercury dipping only into the upper 60s to mid-70s across much of the region. The weather service in Oxnard and San Diego issued extreme heat warnings through 8 p.m. Thursday, cautioning of the risk of heat-related illnesses.
Schoenfeld said a lack of overnight recovery and days of hot weather can “really build and stress the body over time, especially for the elderly and other vulnerable folks like the very young.”
The Los Angeles Department of Public Health is urging residents to hydrate, avoid going outside during the hottest hours of the day, use an umbrella and wear lightweight clothing if you must go out — and take frequent breaks in air conditioned spaces. The county has dozens of cooling centers open.
The heat is expected to relent a bit by the weekend with temperatures in the mid-80s and even a chance of light showers Sunday as Hurricane Rachel continues its path across the Pacific Ocean.
But Swain, the climate scientist, said models suggest that temperatures won’t decline that much as October continues.
“This is not a cool autumn by any means,” he said.

articles.title_orig: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.title_zh: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.content_orig:
The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components.
Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones.
Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices.
The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%.
The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive.
GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World .
“We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.”
In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking.
Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing.
What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint
Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam.
In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026.
“What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels.
The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World.
“ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.”
Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years.
S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025.
Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.
For the world’s poorest consumers, the problem is not simply that smartphones are getting more expensive. It’s that the cheapest phones are disappearing.
The price of a smartphone remains a major barrier for lower-income groups to get online, according to GSMA’s September report. An entry-level device costs the poorest 20% the equivalent of 44% of their monthly income, and 76% for people in sub-Saharan Africa.
When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online.” Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at GSMA’s foundation
For many lower-income consumers, gains in income are unlikely to keep pace with the sudden rise in handset prices.
“When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online. They might delay upgrading, borrow or share their devices, remain on older feature phones, or go offline when they are unable to replace a device that is no longer working or stolen. Often, it means they won’t have an internet-enabled device at all,” Sibthorpe said.
The Saudi wealth fund’s new EV will compete with Chinese rivals and with Lucid, the U.S. carmaker the fund controls.
AI model platforms ModelScope and MoArk are competing to serve Chinese-speaking developers behind the Great Firewall.
