articles.title_orig: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.title_zh: ‘Phoenix planet’ may have formed from a dead star’s ashes
articles.content_orig:
In a cosmic first, scientists say they have detected a planet that may have formed from the burned remains of its dead host star.
The planet is likely a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832 located about 270 light-years from Earth , according to the authors of a study published Monday in the journal Nature Astronomy. After analyzing observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and other instruments, the team found chemical evidence that suggests the planet could have condensed from material expelled by the star as it fizzled out of energy and collapsed into a white dwarf.
When a sunlike star dies, it first rapidly expands into a red giant and then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a much smaller but dense, hot core — known as a white dwarf. Some of the first-generation planets, those that originally formed at the same time as the star, can survive this cataclysmic event if their orbit is wide enough. Astronomers have observed a handful of such first-generation survivors revolving around white dwarfs, but never before have they recorded a so-called second-generation planet — an entirely new world made from a dead star’s debris.
Planet found orbiting a dead star could preview what will happen to our solar system
The telltale sign that HS 0209+0832 might have birthed a new planet is unusual traces of heavy elements on the white dwarf’s surface that the study authors believe is planetary material raining down onto the leftover core. “This planetary material is very rich in an element called niobium,” said lead study author Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in the department of physics of the University of Warwick in England. “It’s the first time that this element is found in a white dwarf, and this implies that the planetary material is made from the ashes of the star as it died.”
Further analysis of observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite or TESS revealed a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days — evidence that the researchers say is consistent with a giant planet orbiting the white dwarf.
“What’s interesting about planets orbiting close to white dwarfs is that because white dwarfs cool over time, their habitable zone is very stable. A second-generation planet could form and then be in the habitable zone for tens of billions of years,” Williams said.
Such a large period of stability could provide more ideal conditions for life, but more work is required to validate the second-generation planet discovery, he added. “It’s not a confirmed planet,” Williams said. “It’s only a candidate for now.”
After the red giant phase when a dying star quickly puffs up, it becomes a nuclear furnace that can produce various elements. However, once that fuel runs out and the star transforms into a white dwarf, the heavy elements — including nobium — sink downward rapidly, leaving only lighter elements such as hydrogen and helium on the surface. The researchers determined that the niobium detected on HS 0209+0832 must therefore come from the star’s surroundings. “We think these elements fell onto the white dwarf’s surface because the white dwarf is very hot and emitting loads of extreme ultraviolet radiation, which is stripping the atmosphere of a nearby planet,” Williams said.
The idea of second-generation planets has existed for at least as long as astronomers have known about exoplanets, said study coauthor David J. Wilson, a research associate at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Scientists detected the very first exoplanets around a pulsar — a type of rapidly rotating dead star — and because pulsars form as a result of massive explosions called supernovas, these planets are likely second-generation, as any original planets would have been destroyed by the immense blast, Wilson explained.
“Although white dwarfs don’t form via supernova, they are surrounded by debris,” he said via email. “You have the planets that were lucky enough to survive the star’s giant phases, the shattered remains of those that weren’t, and leftover gas and dust ejected by the star as it turned from a giant to a white dwarf. So it’s a compelling idea that all that stuff might coalesce into new planets.”
Astronomers still don’t know all the details about how first-generation planets form, which means the potential mechanisms behind this newly reported second-generation planet are even more uncertain. The planet-forming process might have derived from a collision between the dying star and a second celestial body, according to Williams. “There could have been another object close to the core of the star, maybe a star around 20% the mass of the sun, or a brown dwarf,” said Williams, referring to a class of cool objects that are an intermediate between a star and a planet.
If a second object fell into the star during its giant phase, it could have prevented all the dust and gas from spreading out into a massive cloud, making some of it spin in a disk. This disk would then have continued to rotate around the white dwarf, birthing a planet. “In a regular white dwarf there’s no disc, because the star’s material will just be ejected outwards during the red giant phase,” Williams added.
Astronomers discover never-before-seen two-faced star
The researchers plan to use Hubble and NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to observe the system again over the next year, but they also requested time with the more powerful James Webb Space Telescope, which could provide more clues about the existence or features of the planet.
If confirmed, this distant world would belong to an entirely new planetary class and suggest that more second-generation planets could exist around white dwarfs, Williams said.
The discovery would also have implications for our own cosmic neighborhood, Wilson said. “The sun will eventually become a white dwarf, so we’re also looking at the future of the solar system here — maybe the Sun will get a new planet someday!”
The new discovery of a potential second-generation planet is incredibly exciting, said Sarah Casewell, a lecturer at the School of Physics and Astronomy of the University of Leicester, England, who was not involved with the study.
“We know of a large number of white dwarfs that are polluted by planetary material which is similar in composition to rocks within our solar system,” she wrote in an email. “However, in this case, the white dwarf is polluted by incredibly unusual material and the composition of this material is similar to atoms we see being created as stars end their lives.”
More than 95% of all stars in the universe will eventually become white dwarfs, and astronomers have already cataloged hundreds of thousands of them. Finding a planet that has formed after the white dwarf would mean that second-generation planets around other white dwarfs are possible — and that after our sun dies, new planets could emerge in our own solar system, Casewell said.
Radio signal detected for the first time from a planet outside our solar system
Previous observations of white dwarfs have shown that some planetary systems survive a star’s self-destruction, but the recent findings open the possibility of the genesis of new planets, said Amy Bonsor, an associate professor at the University of Cambridge in England, who also did not participate in the work. “This paradigm shift allows us to consider whether in the future we could characterise or investigate the potential habitability of these second-generation planetary systems,” she wrote in an email.
This discovery would also add more evidence to research that has shown planetary systems are varied and complex, even after the host star dies, according to Susan Mullally, a mission scientist at the Space Telescope Science Institute, the science operations center for Hubble.

articles.title_orig: A tropical system is likely in the Gulf this week despite El Niño. Here are the latest scenarios
articles.title_zh: A tropical system is likely in the Gulf this week despite El Niño. Here are the latest scenarios
articles.content_orig:
A tropical depression or storm has a high chance to form in the Gulf this week and breathe life into the tail end of an Atlantic hurricane season squashed by El Niño .
Get live updates and alerts. Download the CNN Weather app.
The Gulf is often a hot bed for late-season storms. Right on cue, chances are increasing for an area of stormy weather festering in the Gulf’s Bay of Campeche to spin up into one by midweek, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The next storm name in the Atlantic is Isaias (ees-ah-EE-ahs).
Exactly where the storm could track or how strong it could get is still up in the air.
Gulf water is record warm for this time of year, primed to generate and help strengthen any system. But this potential storm’s overall strength could be capped by less favorable conditions in the atmosphere.
No matter its final fate, heavy rain is a concern on the Gulf Coast and in other parts of the South by late this week.
All three scenarios are still possible, but it’s looking more likely that a tropical system will form for at least some period of time.
As this year has already shown, it doesn’t take a hurricane-strength system to cause significant impacts, particularly in a warming world that’s making tropical systems wetter.
Tropical storms Arthur and Edouard didn’t last long, but their heavy rain resulted in significant flash flooding and water rescues. Parts of Louisiana and Mississippi took the brunt of Arthur’s flooding while Edouard dropped over 20 inches of rain in eastern Texas.
Parts of Alabama, Georgia, the Florida Panhandle, southeast Louisiana and Mississippi are most at risk of heavy rain from this system. The downpours could start to ramp up along the coast as soon as Friday and then continue to soak the region while creeping farther inland through the weekend.
Several inches of rain could fall, but it’s too soon to pinpoint which locations might see the most and could experience flash flooding.
Four named storms — that’s tropical storm strength or greater — typically form in October and November, but some hurricane seasons can have a stronger finish while others quiet down.
The last few years illustrate this year-to-year ebb and flow. Seven storms formed during October and November in 2024, but just two formed during the same time in 2023.
Late-season storms tend to form closer to the United States, including in the Gulf, Caribbean and off the Southeast coast, which makes them more likely to impact land.
While there are usually fewer storms, they can still be destructive.
Last year, Category 5 Hurricane Melissa devastated Jamaica in October’s final week.
Hurricane Michael roared into the Florida Panhandle on October 10, 2018, becoming the latest landfalling Category 5 on record in the US. And Hurricane Sandy may be the most notorious of all: It morphed into a hybrid superstorm in late-October 2012 and walloped the East Coast.
Super El Niño’s grip on the Atlantic basin means a repeat of notorious late-season hurricanes is less likely this year. Its storm-killing wind is the main reason this season could go hurricane-free for the first time in reliable records .

articles.title_orig: More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may get one-time $90 payment — here's who qualifies
articles.title_zh: More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may get one-time $90 payment — here's who qualifies
articles.content_orig:
More than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries may soon receive a one-time $90 payment from the federal government to offset their Medicare Part B premiums, the White House announced Friday.
President Donald Trump said Friday on Truth Social that his administration will start sending the payments "immediately."
Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary and preventative services, currently has around 62.9 million enrollees, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
About 20.8 million Medicare Part B enrollees will be eligible for the direct payments, according to CMS.
The one-time $90 payment isn't a significant offset for those consumers: For 2026, the standard Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 per month, which works out to about $2,434.80 for the calendar year.
Most eligible seniors will receive a $90 direct deposit payment in early October, according to a White House fact sheet. The payments are separate from the $500 refund checks the administration is sending to Obamacare enrollees.
Most eligible beneficiaries will receive a direct deposit on or around Oct. 8, according to a fact sheet from CMS. Qualifying seniors without direct deposit will receive a check at their mailing address on file with Medicare. Those checks will be sent later in October, according to CMS.
Medicare Part B enrollees who do not qualify include people who get premium assistance from Medicaid and those who pay income-related monthly adjustment amounts — an extra surcharge, also known as IRMAAs , added to monthly premiums for individuals with incomes that exceed certain amounts. Beneficiaries who do not live in the U.S. or who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage are not eligible, either.
The $90 payments will come from unutilized funds in the Medicare Improvement Fund, according to the White House, which has $2 billion authorized by Congress for improvements to Medicare's fee-for-service program.
To check eligibility for the $90 payment, the White House recommends seniors call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227. Beneficiaries may check on their payment status by calling the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213, beginning on Oct. 15.
In 2027, the standard Medicare Part B premium is estimated to increase to $209.50 per month, according to a June report from Medicare's trustees. That's $6.60 more per month than what beneficiaries currently pay, or a $79.20 increase for the year.
Medicare Part B premiums are typically deducted directly from monthly Social Security benefits. As a result, Medicare Part B premium payments affect the increase Social Security beneficiaries see from the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to be announced by the Social Security Administration this month. Experts estimate the annual increase may range from 3.5% to 3.6% based on government inflation data, which would be the highest increase in three years.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s Shield TV Pro just got a $100 price hike
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s Shield TV Pro just got a $100 price hike
articles.content_orig:
﻿The RAMpocalypse’s next victim is a seven year old streaming box.
﻿The RAMpocalypse’s next victim is a seven year old streaming box.
Nvidia’s Shield TV streaming boxes are the latest victims of the memory shortage that has seen prices increase dramatically for everything from digital cameras to game consoles . When the Shield TV Pro launched nearly seven years ago with an upgraded Tegra X1+ processor, 3GB of RAM, and 16GB of storage, it sold for $199.99. But starting on October 2nd Nvidia increased its price by $100 to $299.99 as a result of the increased cost of components, according to Ars Technica .
When the Pro model was first announced in 2019 Nvidia also debuted an updated entry-level version of the Shield TV with the same processor but 2GB of RAM and 8GB of storage priced at $149.99. Unfortunately, it will no longer be an option for those now looking for a cheaper alternative to the Shield TV Pro. Nvidia has stopped production of the standard Shield TV model and moving forward it’s focusing its efforts on only manufacturing the Pro option, according to Gizmodo .
High demand for Nvidia’s other hardware including GPUs and AI chips has been a major contributor to the dramatic price increases of components and devices over the past few years. So while this price increase may reduce demand for the Shield TV Pro while competing streaming boxes like the $149 Google TV Streamer are much cheaper (even after recent price hikes ), it won’t affect Nvidia’s value as the company continues to dominate the AI race.

articles.title_orig: iCloud+ just rolled out an improved perk for subscribers
articles.title_zh: iCloud+ just rolled out an improved perk for subscribers
articles.content_orig:
iCloud+ includes a lot more than additional storage, and one of the service’s perks for subscribers—custom email domains—just got even better.
When creating a new email account, you can always go with a standard @gmail.com or @icloud.com domain. But there’s also a more personalized option.
Third-party services offer custom email addresses at a monthly cost. But unbeknownst to many, iCloud+ lets you create custom email addresses at no extra cost when you own the domain.
With iCloud+, you can set up email addresses that end in something personal to you or your business. It’s one of the service’s most underrated perks, and it just got better.
As detailed by pdfu on X , Apple has now increased the number of email addresses you can create per custom domain.
iCloud+ now lets you use up to 10 personalized email addresses per custom domain.
Previously, you were limited to just 3 personalized addresses per domain. The higher limit of 10 addresses is a big expansion that business owners in particular should appreciate. I’ve also seen plenty of families set up custom domains for their family members, and the higher limit will come in handy for that use case too.
Custom email domains with iCloud+ are available for all subscribers, and you can learn how to set them up here .
Do you use custom email addresses with your iCloud+ subscription? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.title_zh: 'What If the World Had 100 More Mother Cabrinis?' Archbishop Golka Visits Mother Cabrini Shrine
articles.content_orig:
The day before Cabrini Day, Archbishop James Golka made his first official visit to Mother Cabrini Shrine, celebrating a saint whose courage, compassion and missionary faith still challenge Catholics today.
There are certain days at Mother Cabrini Shrine when the past and present seem to come together in a particularly meaningful way. This Cabrini Day is one of them.
As Mother Cabrini Shrine celebrated Colorado’s Frances Xavier Cabrini Day, the Shrine also welcomed Archbishop James Golka for his first official visit — a fitting occasion for the new Archbishop of Denver to visit the holy ground dedicated to a woman whose faith, courage and missionary spirit left such a lasting mark on Colorado.
For Mother Cabrini Shrine, Cabrini Day is much more than a date on the calendar. It is an opportunity to remember the remarkable woman who first came to Denver in 1902 and whose footsteps eventually led her into the foothills west of the city. It was here that Mother Cabrini walked, prayed and cared for the girls from the Queen of Heaven Orphanage. More than a century later, pilgrims continue to come to this same holy ground seeking prayer, peace, healing and a deeper encounter with God.
In 2020, Colorado established Frances Xavier Cabrini Day as a state holiday, observed on the first Monday in October. It became the first paid state holiday in the nation named in honor of a woman — a remarkable distinction and a recognition of the impact Mother Cabrini’s life and work had on Colorado.
But the significance of Cabrini Day extends beyond remembering what Mother Cabrini accomplished more than a century ago. Her life continues to offer an example for the Church and the world today.
Mother Cabrini was a woman of extraordinary faith, but she was also a woman of action. She saw a need and responded. She crossed oceans, overcame obstacles and went wherever she believed God was calling her. Again and again, she said yes — to God, to those who needed her and to the mission placed before her.
(Photo by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
That message was echoed by Archbishop Golka during his homily at the 11:00 a.m. Mass.
Reflecting on Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life and witness, he said: “If the world had 100 more Mother Cabrinis, the faith and the Church would grow in ways that could hardly be imagined.”
He described Mother Cabrini as a woman who had the heart of a mother, caring deeply for those in need and offering an incredible example of faith lived through service. He also spoke about the importance of seeking the intercession of Mother Cabrini and all the saints, expressing his hope that pilgrims who come to the Shrine experience her intercession in their own lives and emphasizing that her witness remains as important today as it was during her lifetime.
That relevance was especially evident as the archbishop referenced “A Pilgrim People, A Shared Home,” an interfaith letter released in conjunction with Cabrini Day, affirming the dignity of every human life, with particular attention to migrant brothers and sisters. The message carries special significance on a day honoring Mother Cabrini, the patron saint of immigrants, whose ministry was shaped by her determination to accompany immigrants and others who found themselves vulnerable or in need.
More than a century later, the circumstances may be different, but Mother Cabrini’s example continues to call people to recognize the dignity of those around them and to respond with compassion.
After Mass, Mother Cabrini Shrine hosted a Festival of Nations that featured traditional music, dance and food from around the world. (Photos by Jonathan Phillips Photography, courtesy of Mother Cabrini Shrine)
Following Mass, Archbishop Golka greeted the faithful before joining the Shrine community for the Festival of Nations. The celebration was filled with joy and color, with foods representing cultures from around the world, people dressed in traditional clothing, and music and dance, including traditional Matachines dancing.
The celebration of nations is especially fitting on Cabrini Day. Mother Cabrini’s own life crossed borders, cultures and languages, and her mission was rooted in welcoming and caring for people far from home. More than a century later, the many cultures gathered together at the Shrine offered a beautiful reflection of both the universality of the Church and the mission she began.
Archbishop Golka’s first official visit was also a reminder that Mother Cabrini Shrine remains very much alive. Her mission continues through the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the clergy who serve the Shrine, its staff and volunteers, and the countless pilgrims who make their way to this holy ground each year. The life and ministry of a place like Mother Cabrini Shrine are sustained by many hands, many hearts and a shared commitment to carrying the mission forward.
Cabrini Day offers an opportunity not only to celebrate Mother Cabrini’s extraordinary life, but also to consider what her example asks of all of us today.
Mother Cabrini saw those who were struggling and moved toward them. She trusted deeply in the Heart of Jesus, relied on prayer and refused to let seemingly insurmountable obstacles keep her from the work God had placed before her.
As Archbishop Golka reminded those gathered at the Shrine, the Church still needs Mother Cabrini. And perhaps one of the greatest ways to honor her is to continue the mission she so courageously began.
For those who have never visited Mother Cabrini Shrine — or perhaps have not been in many years — Cabrini Day offers a wonderful invitation to come and discover the woman behind the name. Walk where she walked, pray where she prayed, learn her story and discover why, more than a century later, St. Frances Xavier Cabrini and her mission still have so much to say to the world today.
Colorado Catholic Conference

articles.title_orig: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals, according to Google
articles.title_zh: When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights for the best deals, according to Google
articles.content_orig:
In trying to score the cheapest airfares for the holidays, when you book a flight often matters just as much as your travel dates. And this year, booking early is particularly important as airfares creep higher, new Google data shows.
Flights for travel around Thanksgiving will be cheapest in October, while people traveling around Christmas should lock in their itineraries by around Halloween, according to Google Flights.
It's best to book as early as possible when your travel dates are relatively fixed. For Thanksgiving, consumers will find the lowest fares 34 days before departure, according to Google Flights, which based its findings on five years of flight data. Thanksgiving is on Nov. 26, making Oct. 22 the best day to book travel for the Wednesday before the holiday. For the lowest fares on Turkey Day trips, travelers should aim to purchase tickets between 57 and 21 days before departure.
For flights around Christmas, the lowest fares will be available 56 days before departure. Travelers can land better deals between 33 and 67 days before their trips, according to Google Flights (as of Oct. 5, there are roughly 80 days before Christmas). The best flight deals will emerge between late October and mid-November, according to Google.
To save money on flights, experts also recommend traveling off-peak, when fewer people will swarm the nation's airports. Data from the fare aggregator Hopper shows that traveling on Monday or Tuesday before Thanksgiving, rather than on Wednesday, can yield savings. Avoid returning on Sunday, Nov. 29, the company said.
The same advice applies around Christmas. Hopper advises avoiding flying on Dec. 18, 19 and 20 and on Dec. 27, the Sunday after Christmas Day.
Americans should expect higher-than-usual flight prices due to the Iran war, which has raised oil and jet fuel prices, the largest expense for airlines after personnel. Before the Middle East conflict began in late February, jet fuel averaged $99 per barrel globally, according to the International Air Transport Association. It peaked at $209 in April and hit $195 a barrel in mid-September, IATA said, citing data from S&P Global Energy Platts.
Hopper data shows that domestic round-trip airfares for Thanksgiving are averaging $402, up 31% from last year. Domestic round-trip Christmas flights are averaging $452, up 23%  from last year.

articles.title_orig: Cornell campus police made drug arrest at Chi Phi fraternity house hours before alleged gang rape
articles.title_zh: Cornell campus police made drug arrest at Chi Phi fraternity house hours before alleged gang rape
articles.content_orig:
Fox News correspondent CB Cotton reports on Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announcing an outside law firm will investigate the school’s response to an alleged 2024 fraternity gang rape on ‘Fox Report.’
Campus police at Cornell University in New York made a drug arrest at the embattled Chi Phi fraternity house on campus less than 24 hours before seven former members are accused in a new civil lawsuit of gang raping a female classmate, according to the school's crime blotter.
The Cornell Daily Sun , an independent campus newspaper at the Ivy League school, resurfaced the daily crime log entry in a new report over the weekend.
Campus police responded to the university-owned frat house around 1 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2024, and arrested a student on drug charges, according to the blotter. It does not include specific charges and indicates that "an individual has been referred to the Office of Student Conduct."
CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS
Police officers respond to an act of vandalism at Day Hall on the campus of Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, Monday, October 5, 2026. The building was vandalized early Monday morning with graffiti amid fallout over the school's response to an alleged sexual assault in 2024. (Everett Chambala / The Cornell Daily Sun)
The blotter does not include details about what type of drug or drugs were involved or whether the arrested individual was a member of Chi Phi. Nor was it immediately clear how the incident was resolved.
Fox News Digital reached out to Cornell for comment and did not immediately receive a response.
CONVICTED RAPIST WHO PREYED ON WOMEN AT AMERICA'S TOP PARTY SCHOOL FACES RECKONING AFTER COURTHOUSE DASH
The fraternity went on to host a party later that day, which stretched into the following morning.
The Chi Phi fraternity house stands on the Cornell University campus in Ithaca, N.Y., on Oct. 2, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
That party is identified in the civil lawsuit filed on behalf of an unidentified Jane Doe, who reported allegations of sexual assault to university police on Nov. 8, telling investigators that she was attacked between 11 p.m. on Oct. 19 and 5:45 a.m. on Oct. 20.
PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE BUST BLOWS LID OFF WIDER STIMULANT SCOURGE HITTING COLLEGE CAMPUSES — AND BEYOND
In Doe's lawsuit, she also alleges she had been pressured into snorting ketamine .
Ketamine is an anesthetic with dissociative and hallucinogenic effects, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration , which also warns that the drug "has also been used to facilitate sexual assault."
THE FRAT OMERTÀ: WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS OF ‘CODE OF SILENCE’ AFTER OLE MISS DEATHS, ALLEGED PENN STATE COKE RING
A sign on the Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)
The fraternity would later be suspended on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sex assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.
Separately, vandals smashed windows and painted slogans in red at Day Hall, an administrative building, early Monday, according to images published by the Daily Sun.
STUDENTS AT TOP PARTY COLLEGE ON EDGE AFTER RAPE, STRANGULATION REPORTED IN CAMPUS HOUSING
"We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community," Kyle Kimball, the school's vice president for university relations, told Fox News in a statement. "Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer. We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law."
Tompkins County prosecutors declined to file criminal charges after Doe first reported the incident to university police in 2024.
FORMER MICHIGAN HOCKEY PLAYERS ALLEGE COACHES IGNORED YEARS OF ABUSIVE HAZING RITUALS
Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University, in New York City, Oct. 2, 2026. (Reuters/Jeenah Moon)
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Doe's November 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped and instead described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
However, according to a local CBS New York report , there is a transcript of what she later told investigators in a two-day interview on Nov. 14 and 15, where she distinguished an initial consensual encounter from allegations of assault that took place later at the party, reportedly telling them, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"Nobody knows this information about the transcript and that gives me something to really dig into because that changes the landscape for me," Van Houten told the outlet.
A general view of Day Hall on the campus of  Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, Monday, October 5, 2026. The building was vandalized early Monday morning with graffiti which would suggest that the attack is in response to an alleged sexual assault in 2024, accused are some members of the Chi Phi fraternity. (Varsha Bhargava / The Cornell Daily Sun)
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor last week to examine the allegations raised in Doe's lawsuit.
Jeremy Saland, the attorney for one of the former fraternity brothers named in the lawsuit, Scott Kretzschmar, told Fox News Digital that his client welcomes "a full and thorough investigation" into Doe's allegations.
"Fairness and justice demand it, and she deserves nothing less," Saland said. "Justice also requires that those entrusted with the investigation reach conclusions from the evidence, not from statements made before the evidence has been reviewed. Though Scott has never been accused of rape, he is confident that an objective and honest process will clear him of any criminal wrongdoing."

Fox News' Ashley Papa, Michael Dorgan and Michelle Langer contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.title_zh: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.content_orig:
PRESS RELEASE — The second international Quantum Datacenter Alliance (QDA) Forum highlighted the progress towards commercial deployments and acceleration of distributed quantum computing architectures, while also outlining the next critical areas of focus for progress.
At the iconic Battersea Power Station, London, the QDA brought together technical, business, and government leaders to address one of the most pressing technical and ecosystem challenges: how to integrate emerging quantum hardware into existing and future data center infrastructure.
The agenda explored how quantum systems are moving from lab-scale demonstrations toward commercial deployment, highlighting that system level architecture, control, error correction, interoperability and power consumption have become as critical as the qubits themselves. Attendees also emphasised the importance of open sharing, interoperability, and collective thinking about the direction and future uses of quantum technologies.
Dr. Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, Founder and CEO of Nu Quantum said, “As quantum computing moves towards large-scale utility, collaboration becomes critical. The QDA brings the industry together to tackle the shared challenges of building quantum computing as infrastructure — scalable, interoperable, reliable and efficient — and ultimately making quantum compute accessible to the world, responsibly.”
Dame Wendy Hall, speaking about lessons from classical computing and AI,said, “It’s all about communication. It is so important to get the positive messages out about any new technology ahead of the inevitable scare stories about the risks and potential harms which the media love to pick up on. Of all the new technologies on the horizon though. Quantum computing is the hardest to explain to non technical audiences. That messaging will need a lot of work as the technology begins to emerge into the public arena.”
Hannah Boardman, Director responsible for AI, Quantum, Engineering Biology, Semiconductors, Robotics, Department for Science, Innovation & Technology , said, “Initiatives like this QDA show the power of bringing together different sections of the ecosystem across technologies, thinking in a different kind of way and focusing on delivering common goals to be identified in the room.”
Petrina Anne Steele, Head of Emerging Technologies at Equinix , said, “Quantum is an incubating technology that sits alongside classical HPC and now AI environments, and is highly complementary. Hybrid infrastructure is making quantum commercially actionable today. We already have companies doing high precision molecular modelling and exploring FX trading optimisation.”
Ben Bloom, Founder and CEO at Atom Computing , said, “Over the past two days, Nu Quantum and its partners have been exploring how to integrate quantum systems into a data center. This is an incredibly important topic as we continue to expand the reach of quantum computers to more and more industries and more and more users. Building a utility scale quantum computer doesn’t just fall to one company, and doesn’t even just fall to one technology. It’s the combination of multiple components together that will actually bring out a utility scale quantum computer.”
Looking ahead, the QDA will continue to convene industry leaders through future forums, working groups, and events, driving the industry toward scalable, robust, commercially viable quantum computing.
Photos can be found from the event here .

NVIDIA Corporation is an American multinational technology company and a global player in accelerated computing and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Founded in 1993, the company pushes the aerospace frontier with the Space-1 Vera Rubin Module, a platform for orbital data centers that delivers massive AI-compute Space Computing. This NVIDIA technology enables satellites and autonomous spacecraft to process and fuse sensor data rapidly Space Computing.
IBM is an iconic technology pioneer founded in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company and officially renamed International Business Machines Corporation in 1924. Beyond foundational computing, IBM possesses a deep legacy in aerospace and defense from building the guidance computers and Instrument Unit for NASA's historic Apollo missions to partnering with Airbus on CIMON, the first AI assistant on the ISS.
II-VI Incorporated, now known as Coherent Corp., is a leading global company specializing in the production of lasers and laser-based solutions. Their extensive product range serves various industrial, commercial, and scientific applications, making their technology integral to numerous sectors and industries.
Equinix specializes in digital infrastructure, operating a global network of data centers that provide colocation, connectivity, and managed solutions for enterprises, cloud providers, and network service providers. The company enables direct, secure interconnection between partners and platforms, supporting mission-critical applications, AI workloads, and hybrid multicloud environments. Equinix emphasizes reliability, scalability, and compliance, serving over 10,000 customers worldwide and facilitating digital transformation through its extensive ecosystem and advanced infrastructure.
Quantinuum is a quantum computing company advancing the aerospace sector through the development of algorithms for aerodynamic modeling, composite materials optimization, and sustainable aviation fuel cell engineering. Founded in 2021 through the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions, the firm provides high fidelity trapped ion hardware and software to accelerate industrial applications.
Atom Computing builds quantum computers using nuclear spin qubits formed from arrays of optically-trapped neutral atoms.
The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) is a department of the government of the United Kingdom. Established in February 2023, DSIT took on policy responsibilities from the former Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. The new department is responsible for helping to encourage, develop and manage the UK's scientific, research, and technological outputs. DSIT is also responsible for managing the necessary physical and digital infrastructure and regulation to support the British economy, UK public services, national security, and wider UK Government priorities.

The DSIT has launched a National Quantum Strategy, which is a 10-year vision and actions for the UK to be a leading quantum-enabled economy, recognizing the importance of quantum technologies for the UK's prosperity and security.
Nu Quantum develops Entanglement Fabric and Quantum Networking Units to interconnect discrete processing cores. Founded in 2018 as a Cambridge University spinout, the company's hardware enables secure quantum networks suitable for aerospace, aviation, and satellite telecommunications, facilitating distributed quantum computing.

The 2026 League of Legends World Championship is almost here. Worlds is the pinnacle of competition, where the best teams from leagues around the globe face off for the ultimate title. This year’s theme is THIS IS OUR MOMENT : Worlds 2026 is more than the culmination of the LoL Esports season, it’s a shared moment a year in the making. THIS IS OUR MOMENT puts everyone at the center of that history. For pros, it’s a chance to push beyond their limits. For fans, it’s a chance to show up and make the moment bigger. For the ecosystem, it’s an opportunity to create the moments we’ll remember for years to come. Because history doesn’t happen without you. Make your moment count.

Worlds has three stages: the Play-In Stage (October 15-18), the Swiss Stage (October 23-31) and the Knockout Stage (November 3-14).
Play-In Stage (Bo5) - Los Angeles, CA All matches begin at 11 AM PDT / 8 PM CEST / 2 AM CST (+1) / 3 AM KST (+1)
Swiss Stage (Bo1, Bo3) - Allen, TX
Knockout Stage (Bo5) - Allen, TX, and Brooklyn, NY

The Play-In Stage will be a four team, best-of-five, double elimination bracket with matchups determined by a fully random draw - any team can play any other team. The draw will take place following the conclusion of the CBLOL Finals on October 10. Teams participating in the Play-Ins are <CBLOL2>, KC, C9, and MVK.

The Swiss Stage is a five-round competition where teams will compete to earn at least three match wins to advance to the Knockout Stage. Teams that accumulate three match losses will be eliminated from the competition.
Matchups for Round 1 will be determined by a random draw following the conclusion of the Play-In Stage on October 18. For the purposes of Round 1, teams have been split into four draw tiers:
Teams from Tier 1 will face teams from Tier 4, while teams from Tier 2 will face teams from Tier 3. Teams from the same region will not be matched against each other in Round 1.
SWISS STAGE ROUND DRAWS - October 23, October 24, October 26, October 30
For Rounds 2 through 5, teams will be paired against random opponents with the same record as them (i.e. 1-0 teams will match against other 1-0 teams). Teams will not be re-matched against a repeat opponent during the Swiss Stage, but same-region matchups are permitted starting with Round 2.
QUARTERFINALS DRAW - October 31
Following the conclusion of  the Swiss Stage, the remaining teams will participate in the Quarterfinals Draw. This draw will randomly pair the two teams with (3-0) Swiss Stage records against two of the teams with (3-2) Swiss Stage records. The remaining four teams will then be randomly drawn into two more matches against one another.

articles.title_orig: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.title_zh: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.content_orig:
Twenty years ago, wind, solar and other non-hydro renewables were close to a rounding error. In 2005 they supplied a mere 2.0% of the world’s electricity generation. By 2015 that had risen to 6.8%, and by 2025 it was up to 19.8%. According to the IEA Electricity 2026 outlook, non-hydro renewables will supply around 21.8% of global electricity in 2026, edging past natural gas (21.6%) to become the second-largest source of power after coal. 1
That is a remarkable pace of growth from an industry that barely existed two decades ago. But not everyone is impressed; many commenters on social media have responded to these figures by pointing out that despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuel generation continues to grow as well. They aren’t wrong; global coal generation set a record in 2024. Gas generation reached a new high in 2025.
Their point is that clean energy isn’t replacing fossil fuels at all. It’s simply being piled on top of them to feed an ever-growing appetite for electricity, making this an “energy addition” rather than an energy transition. Global fossil electricity generation around 50% higher today than it was in 2005. Coal generation rose by 3,300 TWh and gas by 3,200 TWh. The world burns more coal for power now than it did when wind and solar started taking off.
This argument has been made in the past both by skeptics of growth and by energy systems modelers. The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz argues in More and More and More (2024) that “far from the industrial era passing through a series of transformations, each new phase has in practice remained almost wholly entangled with the previous one.” Coal mining created a huge new demand for timber for pit props, while the oil age ran on steel made with coal. Vaclav Smil has made the same point about today’s clean energy boom more bluntly: ”We use more fossil fuels today than at any time in history… Renewables are not replacing fossil fuels; are joining them.”
The problem with the “addition” argument is that it compares the world today with the world in 2005, rather than with the world as it would have been without clean energy. Electricity demand has not grown because wind turbines and solar panels were built. It has grown because of what the IEA describes as “rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centers”. Demand growth is located overwhelmingly in emerging and developing economies, which accounted for about 80% of global demand growth in 2025 and an average of 95% over the past decade.
Global electricity demand rose by 75% (13,600 TWh) between 2005 and 2025. That demand had to be met by something. Wind and solar supplied 5,400 TWh of new demand, hydro 1,500 TWh, bioenergy and other renewables 530 TWh, nuclear 85 TWh, and fossil fuels the remaining 6,100 TWh. But over the past decade the balance has shifted sharply toward clean energy. Since 2015, wind and solar supplied 57% of demand growth, compared with 29% for fossil fuels. And in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 , “wind and solar grew by 841 TWh, meeting 99% of global electricity demand growth”.
A 2024 study by Brantley Liddle found that “intermittent renewables (solar and wind) have unitary displacement effect.” In other words, each unit of wind and solar power displaced about one unit of coal and oil generation. Fossil generation has kept rising in many years because demand has grown faster than clean energy could be added. That is very different from clean energy failing to displace anything.
And electricity demand will continue to rapidly grow, particularly if we succeed in reducing global emissions by electrifying sectors of the economy that currently burn fossil fuels. Most scenarios where we reach net zero emissions involve a doubling or tripling of electricity generation.
So if we want to assess the real world emissions impact of wind and solar buildout over the past 20 years, the right question to ask is not “did fossil use go down?” but rather “how much higher would it have been?”
To answer this, I built a counterfactual for the global power sector in which wind and solar (and geothermal, which is less than 2% of the total) stopped growing in 2005. In every separate country, their generation is held at 2005 levels, while electricity demand, nuclear, hydro and bioenergy follow their real-world paths. 2 The missing clean generation has to come from somewhere, and in this counterfactual it comes from fossil fuels.
The key choice is which fossil fuels are used to fill in the gap. A wind farm in China or India displaces coal, while one in Texas or the UK mostly displaces gas. So rather than assuming a single global fossil mix, the analysis fills each country’s gap with that country’s own coal, gas and oil mix in each year, using data for about 200 countries from Ember . This keeps real-world coal-to-gas switching like what occurred during the US shale gas boom in place, rather than crediting it to renewables. 3
Without wind and solar growth since 2005, global power-sector CO2 emissions in 2025 would have been 28% higher, at 16.9 billion tonnes rather than 13.2 billion. This adds up to 3.7 billion tonnes avoided in 2025, which is about three-quarters of the total CO2 US emissions that year (or roughly 1.5x EU emissions).
Between 2006 and 2025, wind and solar avoided about 23 billion tonnes of CO2. The biggest assumption I’ve made is what fossil fuel fills in the gap: if every missing kilowatt-hour had come from gas, avoided emissions would be 15 billion tonnes, while if it was all coal it would have been 30 billion.
This lines up almost exactly with Ember’s own estimate. Using a simpler method (and a 2000 baseline rather than 2005 baseline), Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 found that “had wind and solar not grown since 2000, fossil generation would have been 30% higher in 2025, and emissions 28% higher.”
While its true that global electricity emissions have yet to clearly peak, it may well be imminent; emissions went down in 2025 and may be on track to decline in 2026 as well, though rapid increases in demand from vehicle electrification and data centers have made this a bit more challenging. 4 But there are many countries in which electricity emissions have already peaked and declined substantially, and where clean energy has played a key role in those declines.
Globally, clean energy has not yet led to fossil fuel use peaking in the electricity sector. In 2025, fossil generation was essentially flat (down ~0.3%). But that global total hides a lot of country-level variability. In many wealthier economies, where demand has grown more slowly, clean energy has driven real emissions reductions (even when accounting for the outsourcing of some industrial production).
Between 2005 and 2025, power-sector CO2 emissions fell by 75% in the UK, 55% in the European Union and 37% in the United States.
The reasons why differ from place to place:
In the EU, wind and solar account for about 85% of the decline (512 of 601 million tonnes), even though falling nuclear output pushed emissions up by about 100 million tonnes.
In the UK, the decline had three main drivers: wind and solar (56 million tonnes), lower domestic generation (58 million tonnes, partly because the UK now imports more power), and the near-elimination of coal, which went from 45% of UK fossil generation to effectively zero (36 million tonnes).
In the US, switching from coal to cheaper natural gas cut emissions by 682 million tonnes, slightly more than wind and solar (606 million tonnes), while a 12% rise in electricity use added 352 million tonnes. Coal’s share of US fossil generation fell from 69% to 29%.
Without wind and solar growth, EU power emissions would have fallen by only about 16% since 2005 rather than 55%, US emissions by about 17% rather than 37%, and UK emissions by about 53% rather than 75%. In these regions clean energy has not just met new demand, its actually pushed fossil generation d

Puerto Rican artist Jay Wheeler has announced the “La Voz Favorita” World Tour, produced by Dynamic Records in partnership with AUL Worldwide and UTA, taking the urban music star to major venues across Europe, the United States and Latin America beginning December 2026.
Presale begins Wednesday, Oct. 7 at 11:00 a.m. local time, while the general onsale starts Friday, October 9 at 11:00 a.m. local time.
“La Voz Favorita” Tour 2026 will kick off in Spain on December 4, 2026, in Tenerife, followed by stops in Gran Canaria, Málaga, Valencia, Bilbao, Madrid and Barcelona, where the European leg will conclude on Dec. 19 with a performance at Palau Sant Jordi.
In March 2027, Wheeler will bring the tour to the United States, with performances in major markets and venues including MGM Music Hall in Boston, Kaseya Center in Miami, Coca Cola Roxy in Atlanta, Fillmore in Denver, YouTube Theater in Los Angeles and many others, with Latin America dates in April and June at markets including Quito, Lima, Tegucigalpa, Guatemala City, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Panama City, San José, Bogotá and Santo Domingo.
“This La Voz Favorita tour is going to be very special. Seeing and hearing all my fans sing along to my songs is one of the most beautiful parts of this career, and I feel truly blessed to have the opportunity to experience it all over again,” said Jay Wheeler.
The tour marks a new chapter in Wheeler’s career, according to the announcement, with Wheeler’s new album seeing multiple hits including “De Lejitos,” which reached No. 1 on Billboard Latin Airplay and Latin Rhythm Airplay, while also reaching No. 7 on Billboard Hot Latin Songs, where it remained in the Top 10 for 11 consecutive weeks.
The booking agency for the tour is AUL Worldwide, with offices in Miami, Los Angeles, Bogotá and Mexico City, led by founder and CEO Adrian Urgelles, who has overseen Jay’s touring alongside with Dynamic Records since 2023.

articles.title_orig: XP Inc. and Other Stocks Surging After Brazil’s Election Shock
articles.title_zh: XP Inc. and Other Stocks Surging After Brazil’s Election Shock
articles.content_orig:
Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown. But this time it is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son Flávio who stands between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and another term in power.
A Bolsonaro victory would push the region further towards the right, hand US President Donald Trump a powerful ideological ally in its largest country and potentially strengthen Washington’s hand as it seeks to counter China’s influence across the hemisphere.
For Lula, 80, the runoff vote leaves one of Latin America’s most prominent left-wing leaders fighting for what is likely will be last term if he wins.
Together, Lula and Bolsonaro accounted for more than 92% of the votes, underscoring the strong grip of the Lula and Bolsonaro camps on Brazilian politics.
But neither secured the 50% needed to avoid a runoff, now set for October 25.
The situation now resembles that of 2022, but Bolsonaro performed better than his father did in the first round four years ago.
The crucial battleground was the Southeast, where nearly 40% of the electorate lives. There, Flávio won São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
His victory in Minas Gerais carries particular symbolic weight: the state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1989 when Brazil held its first direct presidential election after military rule.
The result suggests Bolsonaro, who exceeded poll projections, has done more than simply inherit his father’s political movement. He may have expanded it.
With a campaign focused on crime and the economy, he secured nearly four percentage points more than his father in the first round in 2022. He leaned heavily on his father’s image while also seeking to present himself as a more moderate figure.
For Lula, the result raises an uncomfortable question. Can his political legacy and record in office still deliver an electoral majority?
Minas Gerais helps explain his predicament. He received 43.21% there, well below the 48.3% won in the first round of 2022. Nor did he achieve the lead margin his campaign had hoped for in the Northeast, his main stronghold.
The runoff will depend on who can capture voters who backed eliminated candidates and whether either side can mobilize Brazilians who stayed home on Sunday.
The eliminated candidates collectively accounted for 7.82% of votes.
Most of those votes went to candidates on the center-right or right, potentially giving Bolsonaro another advantage.
But abstention is another potentially decisive reservoir of votes. About 21% of eligible voters did not cast a ballot, and mobilizing them could tip the scales in a tight election.
Polls leading up to Sunday showed the two candidates tied in runoff scenarios.
Lula must now overcome a first-round deficit amid voter concerns over purchasing power and crime, an issue Bolsonaro made central to his campaign, as well as controversies surrounding key figures in scandals seen as close to the president.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, enters the runoff with another advantage: political momentum beyond the presidential race. His party and allies won numerous Senate seats as well as governorships in key states, potentially giving a Bolsonaro presidency significant legislative and regional support.
An even more polarized runoff is expected. Lula will likely frame the vote as a referendum on democracy and while Bolsonaro will focus on his tough-on-crime rhetoric and allegations of corruption against Lula and his party.
Few outside Brazil have more riding on the runoff than Trump. The US president openly endorsed Bolsonaro earlier in the campaign and maintains a tense relationship with Lula’s government.
He has been notably quieter in recent weeks but there is little ambiguity over which outcome would better suit Washington.
Since Trump returned to the White House, no left-wing candidate has won a presidential election in Latin America. Now, Washington hopes to bring about an ideological shift in Brazil, the region’s biggest economy , that will help it fully impose its “Donroe Doctrine” and contain China’s influence.
“Trump had already welcomed Bolsonaro to the Oval Office at the White House and has imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, the sole motivation for which appears to be political,” international relations expert Farid Kahhat, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told CNN.
“The fact that he hasn’t spoken out publicly again doesn’t change the fact that he already did so in the past and that he has made public policy decisions in favor of the Bolsonaros,” he added.
For Kahhat, Trump’s recent restraint may itself be strategic.
“They’ve already decided it was better to keep a lower profile,” he said.
There is good reason for caution. Open intervention by Trump could have the opposite effect in the world’s tenth-largest economy, which is far less dependent on Washington than some of its neighbors.
“They’ve noticed that in Brazil, [interference] might not work the same way as it does in Honduras or Colombia,” Kahhat said.
Lula has also used the banner of national sovereignty as a campaign weapon.
Political scientist Manuel Alcántara Sáez, director of the International Center for Political and Social Studies (CIEPS-AIP) in Panama, said another Trump intervention could end up helping Lula.
“It would be more beneficial for Lula because there is a stronger sentiment against US interference,” he said.
Trump isn’t the only regional ally to have backed Bolsonaro. Argentine President Javier Milei supported him and attended his campaign launch, where he hurled insults at Lula.
“Since then, I haven’t noticed Milei getting so involved in the campaign,” Alexander Main, director of international policy at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told CNN. “I think maybe they felt it wasn’t helping that much.”
But Bolsonaro’s strong showing quickly drew celebration from the Latin American right. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella who won in June with Trump’s backing said on X: “May God have mercy on our brother country as He did on Colombia. True change is defeating the left.”
Milei followed by congratulating Bolsonaro, saying: “The American continent is made up of citizens who want to live in freedom.”
Bolsonaro’s performance appears, at first glance, to fit neatly into Latin America’s broader rightward turn. But analysts caution that something more complicated may be happening.
With strategies based on antagonism and the “cancellation” of the opponent, policy proposals and promises “matter very little” in convincing undecided voters, Alcántara Sáez said.
Beyond the committed bases, “the rest of the electorate is driven by other kinds of impulses, including fatigue and despair at seeing, on one side, an 80-year-old candidate and, on the other, a candidate who is the son of someone in prison, convicted of leading an attempted coup,” he said.
That fatigue echoes a broader pattern across Latin America: incumbent parties struggling to survive voter frustration.
Kahhat said that although “this is a time of crisis for the left throughout the region,” the string of right-wing victories should not necessarily be read as a wholesale ideological conversion.
“It depends on the context, but it is not necessarily a rejection of left-wing movements as such, but rather of those in power at a time of great economic instability,” he said.
Brazil’s runoff will therefore test two competing explanations for the political transformation sweeping the region: whether Latin America is undergoing a durable shift to the right, or whether frustrated voters are simply punishing whoever happens to be in power.
For Alcántara Sáez, there is another dividing line that may prove just as important: how Latin American governments position themselves toward Trump.

articles.title_orig: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
articles.title_zh: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
articles.content_orig:
It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.
Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country.
The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism.
The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally.
What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.
Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed.
Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion.
The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin.
So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy.
Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership.
And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership.
In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy.
The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections.
It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy.
Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham.
In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term.
While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard".
Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc.
And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum."
Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda.

articles.title_orig: Celebrating World Teachers’ Day: The Mentors Who Help Young Scientists Find Their Voice
articles.title_zh: Celebrating World Teachers’ Day: The Mentors Who Help Young Scientists Find Their Voice
articles.content_orig:
Today, October 5, communities around the globe are celebrating World Teachers’ Day, a moment to recognize the teachers who show up every day to spark curiosity, build confidence and help young people imagine what they can become.
Educators do far more than deliver lessons. They notice the quiet student with a big question, bring to their attention opportunities students didn’t know existed, and stay late to help an experiment finally work.
At Society for Science, educators are at the heart of so much of what we do. Behind nearly every young researcher who steps up to a science fair board, enters a competition or presents their findings to a judge, there is a teacher or mentor who encouraged them. Anna Pawlow, the Society’s Director of STEM Literacy & Curriculum says, “Our STEM Outreach programs recognize that teachers are the experts in effective STEM education and student research. That is why the peer-to-peer learning model is at the core of our teacher professional development programming. We celebrate educators’ immeasurable impact by creating meaningful opportunities for them to learn from one another, build community and inspire new possibilities for their students.”
This World Teachers’ Day, we asked three educators who work closely with Society for Science to share their thoughts on STEM education.
Allyson McFalls ELA & Science Teacher, Blowing Rock School Blowing Rock, North Carolina
Allyson has participated in the Society’s Advocate Program as an Advocate and a Lead Advocate. She is also a former Western North Carolina STEM Research Ambassador, leading the Society’s NC STEM Research Fellow Program. Allyson participates in the Science News Learning program and has mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
For many students, especially adolescents, time in the classroom can feel like an obligation, not a joy. My goal with implementing independent research experiences is to provide students the opportunity to explore in depth a subject that matters deeply to them, and in the process discover that there is joy in deep learning. Helping students discover the project that fits them is key to helping them engage with the rest of our science content and helps them see that I care about them as more than a data point—as an individual with unique interests and passions.
Can you tell us about a time when a student’s confidence or trajectory changed because of a research experience?
I’ve had the joy of teaching students in both 6th and 8th grade in a small rural school. There are a few girls who entered 6th grade very hesitant about their science skills and aptitude, worried about whether they could “do it” when it came to science fair projects. Watching them discover their passion through science fair has been incredible, and now, as 8th-grade students, they are not only confident in their own research, but are actively seeking out opportunities and connections to build their science education. I can’t wait to see how their lives unfold!
Milene de Farias Teacher, Southcrest Christian School Lubbock, Texas
Milene has participated in the Society’s Research Teachers Conference, served as an Invention Fellow and participates in the Science News Learning program. She has also mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF, as well as in Thermo Fisher JIC, Regeneron ISEF and Regeneron STS.
What drew you to teaching, and specifically to teaching a STEM subject? Was there a teacher or mentor in your own life who shaped how you teach today?
In 6th grade, I moved to a traditional public school, where my science teacher introduced me to a real lab for the first time and I took part in a science fair. I was shy, but when it came to my projects, I could talk with anybody who asked about them, and I couldn’t wait to start researching for my 7th-grade project.
The science fair changed my plans of becoming a model, a surfer or a crime novel writer, and I chose to attend a technical STEM high school. There, my math teacher, Armando, made a lasting impact on how I teach. He taught with empathy and always used projects. I still remember learning trigonometry by going outside to measure the height of our four-story school building, which is why I love hands-on activities today.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
Information is everywhere today, and students can find an answer in seconds, but personal experiences are what truly shape them. When students choose a problem they care about and work to solve it, they build critical thinking, curiosity and grit, because real research does not always go as planned. They learn to ask better questions and keep going when the results surprise them. Independent research also connects students to the needs of their community, which teaches them to think beyond themselves and see that science can make a difference.
Oktay Ince Director of Teaching and Learning, Concept Schools Columbus, Ohio
Oktay has participated in the Society’s Advocate Program as an Advocate and a Lead Advocate. He has also attended the Research Teachers Conference as an attendee and a Captain, participated in the Science News Learning program and mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF.
What drew you to teaching, and specifically to teaching a STEM subject? Was there a teacher or mentor in your own life who shaped how you teach today?
I believe teaching is rewarding both personally and professionally. I think it is especially rewarding when you are teaching in a STEM field. You know that you are making a difference in the lives of students—their life trajectories, their families and the communities around them.
Witnessing this makes my heart full of joy. It makes me think that I am leaving a legacy in this world, even after I am gone. That is what makes teaching so meaningful to me. This servant mindset was instilled in me by my parents, teachers and coaches. They taught me that our purpose is not only to be successful ourselves, but also to help others become successful. That is the mindset I try to bring to my students every day.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
I believe acquiring skills through the experience of conducting independent research is one of the highest forms of education we can give to students.
Students do not have to choose a career in STEM, but the skills they develop through the research process can set them up for success in almost anything they choose to do. They learn how to ask questions, solve problems, think critically, communicate, persevere when things do not work and defend their ideas.
Independent research experiences are both transformative and transferable.
If we want our students to be prepared for a constantly changing world and to be competitive in that world, I believe students from all backgrounds need opportunities to experience independent research. We are not just preparing them for a science fair or a STEM career. We are preparing them to become thinkers, problem-solvers, and people who believe they can make a difference.

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.content_orig:
U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”
You can read more about The Princeton Review’s methodology here .
